title: Past Questions — Compiled from the Net

sets.title: Set 01
sets.subtitle: Original two-section examination · True/False and MCQs

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricle increases during

options.label: D
options.text: Sympathetic stimulation that raises heart rate and contractility.

options.label: E
options.text: A rise in perfusion pressure within the autoregulatory range.

notes.A: Contraction of ventricular muscle compresses left coronary vessels early in systole and reduces inflow, especially in deeper wall layers.
notes.B: Myocardial hypoxia promotes release of local vasodilators, including adenosine, which increase flow if coronary reserve is available.
notes.C: Cooling typically lowers myocardial metabolic demand, reducing the stimulus for coronary vasodilatation and increased flow.
notes.D: A rise in heart rate and contractility raises myocardial oxygen demand. Local metabolic vasodilatation generally increases flow despite direct adrenergic effects.
notes.E: Within the autoregulatory range, coronary resistance changes with perfusion pressure and keeps steady-state flow relatively constant.

questions.why: Most left-ventricular coronary inflow occurs during diastole because systolic muscle contraction compresses intramural vessels. Local metabolic vasodilatation increases flow when myocardial oxygen demand outstrips delivery.

questions.stem: Ventricular filling

options.label: C
options.text: Gives rise to a third heart sound in some healthy people.

options.label: D
options.text: Can occur only when atrial pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure.

options.label: E
options.text: Is most rapid in the first half of diastole

notes.A: Most filling at a normal resting rate is passive. Atrial contraction adds a variable portion near the end of diastole.
notes.B: During isovolumetric relaxation inflow and outflow valves are closed. Filling starts only once an atrioventricular valve opens.
notes.C: Rapid early filling can produce an audible third heart sound, which may be physiological in young people or pregnancy.
notes.D: The atrium need only exceed the ventricle in pressure. Absolute pressure relative to the atmosphere does not determine valve opening.
notes.E: The atrioventricular pressure gradient is initially greatest in early diastole, and filling slows later during diastasis.

questions.why: Ventricular filling begins when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure and the atrioventricular valves open. Rapid passive filling occurs first, with atrial contraction contributing near end-diastole.

questions.stem: In the heart

options.label: A
options.text: The left atrial wall is about three times thicker than the right atrial wall.

options.label: B
options.text: Systolic contraction normally begins in the left atrium.

options.label: C
options.text: Excitation spreads directly from atrial muscle cells to ventricular muscle cells.

options.label: D
options.text: Atrial and ventricular muscle contracts simultaneously in systole.

options.label: E
options.text: The contracting ventricles shorten from apex to base.

notes.A: The left atrial wall is only slightly thicker than the right; the threefold difference applies to the ventricles (LV vs RV).
notes.B: Excitation starts at the SA node in the right atrium, so the right atrium is activated first.
notes.C: The fibrous skeleton insulates atria from ventricles; the only normal electrical path is the AV node and bundle of His.
notes.D: Atrial systole comes first (about 0.1-0.2 s before ventricular systole), giving the AV nodal delay time for atria to top up the ventricles.
notes.E: As the ventricles contract, the base (AV ring) is pulled down towards the apex, shortening the long axis of the ventricles.

questions.why: The beat starts at the SA node in the right atrium and reaches the ventricles only through the AV node and His bundle, so atria contract before ventricles and the base is pulled toward the apex.

questions.stem: The net loss of fluid from capillaries in the legs is increased by

options.label: B
options.text: Change from the recumbent to the standing position.

notes.A: Arteriolar dilatation transmits more pressure to downstream capillaries and increases the outward hydrostatic driving force.
notes.B: Standing adds a gravitational pressure head to vessels below the heart, raising venous and capillary pressure in the legs.
notes.C: Lymphatic blockage primarily prevents return of filtered fluid and protein. The resulting oedema does not require an immediate increase in capillary filtration.
notes.D: A venous obstruction raises upstream venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure, promoting outward fluid transfer.
notes.E: Lower albumin reduces the plasma oncotic force opposing filtration and favours net fluid loss from capillaries.

questions.why: Fluid filtration increases when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises or plasma oncotic pressure falls. Lymphatic return normally clears filtered fluid, so failure of drainage can cause accumulation independently.

questions.stem: When measuring blood pressure by the auscultatory method

options.label: A
options.text: The sounds that are heard are generated in the heart.

options.label: B
options.text: The cuff pressure at which the first sounds are heard when deflating the cuff indicate systolic pressure.

options.label: C
options.text: The cuff pressure at which the loudest sounds are heard indicate diastolic pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: Systolic pressure estimations tend to be lower than those made by the palpatory method.

options.label: E
options.text: Wider cuffs are required for larger arms.

notes.A: The pulse distends the partly compressed brachial artery and generates vibrations in nearby tissue. The sounds arise locally.
notes.B: The first tapping sounds appear as cuff pressure falls just below peak arterial pressure and intermittent flow resumes.
notes.C: Diastolic pressure usually corresponds to disappearance of the sounds. The loudest phase is not the standard endpoint.
notes.D: A palpable distal pulse may return only after some flow is restored. An auscultatory gap can also cause error if missed.
notes.E: A larger arm needs a proportionately larger cuff bladder. A cuff that is too small can overestimate pressure.

questions.why: As an upper-arm cuff deflates, the first Korotkoff sounds mark systolic pressure and their disappearance usually marks diastolic pressure. The correct cuff size helps avoid systematic error.

questions.stem: Vascular resistance

options.label: A
options.text: Increases by 50 per cent when the vascular radius is halved.

options.label: B
options.text: Is related to the thickness of the wall of the vessel.

options.label: C
options.text: Is related to the state of contraction of the smooth muscles in vessel walls.

options.label: E
options.text: Is greater in the capillary bed than in the arteriolar bed.

notes.A: For ideal laminar flow in a tube, resistance varies inversely with radius to the fourth power. Halving radius increases resistance sixteenfold.
notes.B: Wall thickness affects mechanics, but it is the lumen radius that enters the basic resistance relation when other flow conditions are fixed.
notes.C: Contraction of vascular smooth muscle narrows the lumen and increases resistance. Relaxation tends to have the opposite effect.
notes.D: Higher viscosity increases resistance for a given vessel geometry because more pressure is needed to sustain the same flow.
notes.E: Each capillary has a narrow lumen, but many lie in parallel. Arterioles normally account for a larger pressure drop.

questions.why: Vascular resistance depends strongly on lumen radius and also on blood viscosity and vessel length. Arteriolar smooth muscle changes resistance dynamically by changing lumen size.

questions.stem: Sympathetic drive to the heart is increased,

options.label: D
options.text: When emotions stimulate the pressor area of the vasomotor centre.

options.label: E
options.text: During a sudden a sudden increase in blood pressure.

notes.A: Exercise raises sympathetic output, helping accelerate the cardiac pacemaker and increase ventricular contractile force.
notes.B: Excitement can activate central autonomic pathways and increase sympathetic stimulation of the heart.
notes.C: Hypotension reduces stretch and firing in arterial baroreceptors, increasing reflex sympathetic outflow to the heart.
notes.D: Limbic and hypothalamic activity can recruit medullary cardiovascular pathways during emotions, increasing adrenergic drive.
notes.E: A sudden pressure rise increases baroreceptor firing and typically decreases sympathetic drive while increasing cardiac vagal activity.

questions.why: Central command and autonomic reflexes increase cardiac sympathetic drive during exercise, excitement and hypotension. A sudden arterial pressure rise activates baroreceptors and normally reduces that drive.

questions.stem: In the electrocardiogram, the

options.label: A
options.text: QRS complex follows the onset of ventricular contraction.

options.label: B
options.text: T wave is due to repolarization of the ventricles.

options.label: C
options.text: PR interval corresponds with atrial depolarization.

options.label: D
options.text: QT interval approximates the duration of the ventricular action potential.

options.label: E
options.text: R-R interval normally varies during the respiratory cycle

notes.A: Ventricular depolarisation produces the QRS complex and precedes force generation in the ventricular muscle.
notes.B: The T wave reflects the net electrical effect of ventricular repolarisation after the myocardium is activated.
notes.C: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave. The PR interval also includes conduction of the impulse toward the ventricles.
notes.D: From QRS onset to the end of the T wave, the QT interval approximates the period of ventricular electrical activity.
notes.E: In respiratory sinus arrhythmia, the rate usually rises during inspiration and falls during expiration as vagal activity varies.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves
questions.why: The electrocardiogram records electrical activation and recovery before their mechanical consequences. The PR interval includes atrioventricular conduction, while the QT interval spans ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation.

questions.stem: The tendency for blood flow to be turbulent increases when there is a decrease in blood

options.label: A
options.text: Vessel diameter, with flow velocity held constant.

questions.why: Flow is more prone to turbulence when the Reynolds number rises. For a given velocity and vessel diameter, lower viscosity increases Reynolds number by weakening viscous damping.

notes.A: At fixed velocity, a smaller vessel diameter lowers Reynolds number. This makes turbulence less likely, other factors being equal.
notes.B: Lower density reduces inertial forces relative to viscous forces, decreasing Reynolds number at the same velocity and diameter.
notes.C: Slower flow reduces inertial forces relative to viscous forces and lowers the tendency toward turbulence.
notes.D: Lower viscosity provides less damping of flow disturbances and increases Reynolds number when other variables are held constant.
notes.E: Anaemia generally reduces blood viscosity and can increase flow velocity through higher cardiac output. Both changes favour flow murmurs.

questions.stem: In the estimation of cardiac output using the Fick principle

options.label: B
options.text: The PO2 of arterial and mixed venous blood are measured.

options.label: C
options.text: Oxygen uptake is estimated from alveolar PO2 measurements.

options.label: D
options.text: Pulmonary arterial blood is sampled to measure the oxygen in mixed venous blood.

options.label: E
options.text: Pulmonary venous blood is sampled to measure the oxygen in arterial blood.

questions.why: The Fick principle gives CO = O2 uptake / (arterial O2 content - mixed venous O2 content).

notes.A: It measures the blood flow through the lungs, which equals cardiac output when there are no shunts.
notes.B: O2 CONTENTS (mL O2 per L blood) are used, not partial pressures; PO2 alone ignores haemoglobin-bound oxygen.
notes.C: Whole-body O2 uptake is measured from inspired and expired gas volumes and concentrations (spirometry), not from alveolar PO2.
notes.D: Properly mixed venous blood is sampled from the pulmonary artery via a catheter.
notes.E: Pulmonary venous blood has the same O2 content as systemic arterial blood; in practice any systemic artery is sampled instead.

questions.stem: What is Starling's Law that applies to activity in both skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle? It states that

options.label: A
options.text: there more Ca²⁺ released among the myofibrils the greater the power of contraction observed in the muscle

options.label: B
options.text: the tension generated in a contracting muscle increases exponentially as the muscle is stretched

options.label: C
options.text: within a limited range of length change the more one stretches the muscle before it contracts the greater the tension generated

options.label: D
options.text: ventricular heart working cell is able to generate a stronger contraction the more blood it is perfused with

options.label: E
options.text: the more pressure there is on the muscle the greater is its ability to overcome the pressure

questions.why: Starting muscle length affects the active tension generated. Within the ascending part of the length–tension relation, stretching increases force, helping the heart match stroke volume to ventricular filling.

notes.A: Increased available calcium can raise force at a fixed length. That is a change in activation, not the length–tension relation.
notes.B: Active tension depends on initial length and eventually falls beyond an optimal range. It does not increase exponentially with stretch.
notes.D: Coronary perfusion supplies the myocardium with oxygen. It is ventricular filling that increases initial fibre stretch in the Starling response.
notes.E: Pressure against the muscle reflects its load. Greater load generally reduces shortening if initial length and activation are unchanged.

questions.stem: What principle enables the use of the sphygmomanometer and the stethoscope to measure blood pressure in clinical practice?

options.label: A
options.text: Fluid flow in large tubes is laminar and silent but narrowing causes turbulent noisy flow

options.label: B
options.text: The blood flow through arteries hit the walls and generate sound at different frequencies

options.label: C
options.text: The narrowing of the blood vessels by the balloon cuff accentuates the sounds already present

options.label: D
options.text: The thick arterial walls vibrate as they get partially occluded

options.label: E
options.text: There is no simple explanation to the use of the equipment

questions.why: Blood flows silently (laminar) through an open artery. When the cuff partly compresses the artery, blood spurts through the narrowing at high velocity and becomes turbulent, producing the Korotkoff sounds heard with the stethoscope.

notes.B: Normal laminar arterial flow does not make audible sounds.
notes.C: There are no sounds to accentuate; the cuff creates them.
notes.D: Wall vibration happens, but it is driven by turbulent flow through the narrowing.
notes.E: Turbulence explains the method.

questions.stem: What statement is valid to describe what will happen to the heart if all its extrinsic nerves are cut?

options.label: B
options.text: The heart may still beat adequately to sustain life

options.label: C
options.text: The rate of the heart beats can no longer be changed

options.label: D
options.text: The heart function will become more efficient

options.label: E
options.text: No heart sounds will be heard with a stethoscope

questions.why: Sinoatrial pacemaker cells generate impulses intrinsically, so a denervated heart can keep beating and sustain circulation. Neural input normally adjusts its rate and force to demand.

notes.A: Pacemaker depolarisation is intrinsic to the sinoatrial node, so loss of extrinsic nerve supply does not stop the heart.
notes.C: Circulating catecholamines can still change rate in a denervated heart, although rapid neural control is lost.
notes.D: Removing neural input reduces the speed and range of autonomic adjustments. It does not inherently improve pumping efficiency.
notes.E: Heart sounds result from vibrations associated with mechanical events, especially valve closure, which continue in a beating denervated heart.

questions.stem: Which statement is the best description for cardiac output? The cardiac output

options.label: A
options.text: is the work done by the heart in pumping out blood in a minute

options.label: B
options.text: is the volume of blood the heart pumps to either the pulmonary circulation or the peripheral circulation

options.label: C
options.text: of an animal will equal all the blood that will come out of its cut aorta in a minute

options.label: D
options.text: equals the total blood volume pumped out by a ventricle in an individual exercising

questions.why: Cardiac output is the volume delivered by one ventricle per unit time, usually one minute. It equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

notes.A: Work or energy transfer per minute describes power. Output here measures volume per time rather than energy per time.
notes.C: Opening the aorta would change pressures and circulatory conditions, so the resulting bleeding rate cannot define normal cardiac output.
notes.D: Cardiac output applies at rest and during exercise. The total volume also needs a specified time interval.
notes.E: The volume delivered by one ventricle to its circulation per minute gives the definition represented among the choices.

questions.stem: What is the state of valves just after left ventricular systole has started during the cardiac cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: The mitral valve is open and the aortic valve is open

options.label: B
options.text: The mitral valve is closed and the aortic valve is closed

options.label: C
options.text: The mitral valve is open and the aortic valve is closed

options.label: D
options.text: The state of the valves can only be known if sympathetic activity is known

questions.why: At the start of left ventricular systole, rising ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve. The aortic valve opens later, after ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure.

notes.A: The mitral valve closes before ventricular ejection. The aortic valve does not open until pressure builds sufficiently.
notes.C: An open mitral valve with a closed aortic valve is the usual filling configuration during ventricular diastole.
notes.D: Pressure differences determine valve position. The normal early systolic interval can be identified without information about sympathetic activity.
notes.E: Both valves are closed during isovolumetric contraction, allowing ventricular pressure to rise at constant chamber volume.

questions.stem: Which muscle cell membrane property allows all parts a ventricle to depolarize rapidly?

options.label: E
options.text: Sarcoplasmic reticulum sacs of calcium ions

questions.why: Gap junction channels allow depolarising current to pass between neighbouring ventricular myocytes. Their low-resistance coupling helps activation spread rapidly through myocardium after the conducting system delivers the impulse.

notes.B: Intercalated discs contain mechanical contacts as well as gap junctions. The gap junction channels specifically provide electrical coupling.
notes.C: Mitochondria supply metabolic energy for ion transport and contraction. They do not carry depolarising current into adjacent cells.
notes.D: The Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins inside each cell. It does not provide a direct electrical route between cells.
notes.E: Sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium to activate contraction after depolarisation. It does not conduct the depolarisation from cell to cell.

questions.stem: The following relax smooth muscle in the systemic arteriole and allow more blood to flow through EXCEPT

options.label: C
options.text: an increase in the amount of heat

questions.why: Endothelin released by vascular endothelium generally constricts systemic resistance vessels by activating smooth muscle receptors. Local metabolites and nitric oxide often favour dilation instead.

notes.A: Carbon dioxide can accumulate in active tissue and contribute to local systemic vasodilatation, increasing perfusion to the area.
notes.B: A lower local pH often accompanies increased metabolism and can relax resistance vessels in systemic tissues.
notes.C: Local warming can increase cutaneous flow through vasodilatation, helping transfer excess heat to the surroundings.
notes.E: Endothelial nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle and promotes relaxation through cyclic GMP.

questions.stem: These factors oppose fluid filtration out of the circulation EXCEPT
questions.why: Capillary hydrostatic pressure is the main force pushing fluid OUT of capillaries, so it promotes filtration rather than opposing it.

notes.A: Plasma oncotic pressure (mainly albumin) pulls fluid back into capillaries.
notes.B: A positive tissue fluid (interstitial hydrostatic) pressure pushes against filtration.
notes.D: In this question's Starling framework, lymphatic and tissue-side pressure is counted as opposing filtration.
notes.E: C is clearly an exception.

questions.stem: The normal functions of the heart include all of the following EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: secreting a hormone that promotes renal salt loss

options.label: B
options.text: generating the pressure gradient that drives blood flow

options.label: C
options.text: keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate

options.label: D
options.text: acting as the body's main reservoir of blood volume

options.label: E
options.text: sensing blood volume through atrial stretch receptors

questions.why: The heart creates the pressure gradients for pulmonary and systemic flow and also has sensory and endocrine functions. The systemic venous circulation contains the main blood-volume reservoir.

notes.A: Stretch of atrial myocytes promotes secretion of atrial natriuretic peptide, which supports sodium excretion by the kidneys.
notes.B: Ventricular contraction generates pressure differences that drive blood through pulmonary and systemic vascular beds.
notes.C: The atrial and ventricular septa form a barrier that separates the systemic and pulmonary blood streams in the normal heart.
notes.E: Atrial stretch receptors sense filling and participate in autonomic and endocrine responses to changes in blood volume.

questions.subtopic: Functions of the heart and circulation

questions.stem: Select the valid statement about the patterns of blood flow in the systemic and pulmonary circulations

options.label: A
options.text: Pulmonary arteries carry blood with a higher PO₂ than the pulmonary veins

options.label: B
options.text: Coronary sinus blood has a higher O₂ content than mixed venous blood

options.label: C
options.text: Aortic flow per minute is slightly less than pulmonary arterial flow

options.label: D
options.text: Pulmonary arterioles constrict when the PO₂ of the alveolar gas falls

options.label: E
options.text: Systemic arterioles constrict when the PO₂ of the tissue fluid falls

questions.why: Low alveolar oxygen causes constriction of nearby pulmonary arterioles. This response redirects blood away from poorly ventilated regions and helps match ventilation to perfusion.

notes.A: Pulmonary arteries carry mixed venous blood into the lungs. Pulmonary veins normally carry more oxygenated blood away.
notes.B: The myocardium extracts a large share of delivered oxygen, so coronary sinus blood usually has less oxygen than mixed venous blood.
notes.C: In steady state the ventricular flows are close. Bronchial venous drainage into the left heart can make left-sided flow slightly greater.
notes.E: In most systemic tissues, lower local oxygen favours arteriolar dilatation and increases blood flow to restore delivery.

questions.stem: All these regions of the heart have the ability to generate measurable electrical activity EXCEPT
questions.why: Nodal cells, conducting fibres and working myocardial cells all generate electrical activity. Surface ECG chiefly represents summed myocardial activity, while specialised conduction signals can be recorded intracardially.

notes.A: Sinoatrial cells produce spontaneous pacemaker action potentials that normally set heart rate.
notes.B: Atrioventricular nodal cells produce action potentials and carry impulses slowly between atria and ventricles.
notes.C: Activation of atrial and ventricular working myocytes provides much of the deflection measured on the body surface.
notes.D: The bundle of His conducts impulses toward the bundle branches. Its local electrical signal can be recorded intracardially.

questions.stem: Which of the following is FALSE concerning the regulation of heart muscle performance?

options.label: A
options.text: Recruiting more numbers of motor units will increase the strength of contraction.

options.label: B
options.text: Increases in end-diastolic volume will generate a larger stroke volume during systole.

options.label: C
options.text: The amount and duration of Ca released from the SR can alter contractility.

options.label: D
options.text: Positive inotropic agents will increase contractility

options.label: E
options.text: Adrenaline increases the contractility of working heart muscles

questions.why: Cardiac excitation spreads through electrically coupled myocytes rather than recruiting skeletal motor units. Ventricular force varies with initial fibre length and calcium availability to the myofilaments.

notes.B: Greater filling stretches cardiac muscle and can increase stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism within the physiological range.
notes.C: The cytosolic calcium transient depends partly on sarcoplasmic reticulum release. Changing that transient can alter the strength of contraction.
notes.D: Positive inotropic agents increase force at a given initial muscle length, reflecting enhanced contractility.
notes.E: Adrenaline stimulates cardiac beta-1 receptors and increases calcium availability, strengthening ventricular contraction.

questions.stem: Individual capillaries have narrow lumens but the capillary beds offer the least resistance to blood flow because

options.label: B
options.text: several capillaries in parallel offer a large cross sectional area to blood flow

options.label: C
options.text: several capillaries in series offer adequate length for blood flow

options.label: D
options.text: all precapillary sphincters are either opened or closed

options.label: E
options.text: there is too little blood going through the capillaries at any one time

questions.why: Capillaries are arranged in vast numbers in parallel, so their combined cross-sectional area is huge (about 1000 times that of the aorta). Resistances in parallel add as reciprocals, so total resistance stays low and flow velocity is slow, which helps exchange.

notes.A: Capillaries do lack valves, but that does not explain low resistance.
notes.C: Vessels in series add resistance.
notes.D: Precapillary sphincters open and close at different times, not all together.
notes.E: The whole cardiac output passes through the capillaries.

questions.stem: How many red blood cells can fit into the width of a capillary?
questions.why: In a typical narrow systemic capillary, red blood cells pass in single file. Their deformable membranes allow them to squeeze through lumens comparable to, or smaller than, their resting diameter.

notes.B: Two erythrocytes can be present at different points along a capillary, but the typical lumen is too narrow for them to pass side by side.
notes.C: Three cells abreast need a wider lumen than an ordinary capillary. The cells typically align one behind another.
notes.D: Four cells across would require a substantially wider vessel. A typical capillary accommodates erythrocytes in single file.
notes.E: Five erythrocytes abreast are incompatible with the narrow lumen of a typical exchange capillary.

questions.stem: Which vessels in the vasculature begin as ‘blind-ended’ tubes?
questions.why: Initial lymphatic vessels begin as blind-ended channels in tissue. Overlapping endothelial edges can open when interstitial pressure rises, admitting fluid and macromolecules into the lymphatic network.

notes.A: Blood capillaries usually form a connected exchange network between arterioles and venules. They do not collect interstitial fluid through blind ends.
notes.B: Sinusoids are specialised wider blood channels, such as those linking inflow to central veins in the liver.
notes.C: Venules receive blood from capillaries and carry it toward veins. They are part of a continuous blood circuit.
notes.E: Coronary arteries arise from the aorta and branch toward myocardial exchange vessels. They do not begin in the interstitium.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to produce delayed diastolic filling of the left ventricle?

options.label: E
options.text: increasing heart rate from 80 to 100 beats/min

questions.why: Mitral stenosis obstructs flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle. It imposes a diastolic pressure gradient across the valve and slows ventricular filling.

notes.A: Aortic stenosis obstructs systolic outflow. Later ventricular hypertrophy can affect relaxation, but the valve lesion does not directly obstruct mitral inflow.
notes.B: Tricuspid regurgitation permits backward flow from the right ventricle during systole. It does not directly narrow left ventricular inflow.
notes.D: Pulmonary stenosis impedes flow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery. It is downstream of the tricuspid valve.
notes.E: A faster rate shortens diastole and may limit total filling time. It does not produce the direct inflow obstruction of mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors contribute(s) to the maintenance of balance between the outputs of the left and right ventricles?
questions.why: If one ventricle ejects more blood, the other receives more filling over subsequent beats. The Frank–Starling response increases stroke volume with preload and helps restore balance.

notes.A: Sympathetic input changes contractility and heart rate and can adjust overall flow. The intrinsic matching response to increased filling does not require it.
notes.B: Parasympathetic input mainly adjusts nodal activity and heart rate. It is not the intrinsic link between filling and ventricular output.
notes.C: Circulating adrenaline can increase ventricular contractility. Matching of each ventricle’s output to its own filling does not depend on an adrenaline change.
notes.E: The named intrinsic filling–output relation accounts for the matching. Autonomic and adrenal influences can modify performance but are not all required.

questions.stem: During the rapid ejection phase of the cardiac cycle:

options.label: D
options.text: ventricular volume is at its lowest volume

options.label: E
options.text: the first heart sound starts during this phase

questions.why: Rapid ejection starts when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure and opens the aortic valve. Aortic inflow initially exceeds peripheral runoff, so aortic pressure rises.

notes.A: The mitral valve remains closed while left ventricular pressure exceeds left atrial pressure. It opens later when the ventricle relaxes.
notes.C: The aortic valve is open during ventricular ejection, allowing blood to enter the aorta from the ventricle.
notes.D: Ventricular volume falls during rapid and then reduced ejection. It reaches its lowest value at end-systole.
notes.E: The first heart sound begins around atrioventricular valve closure, during isovolumetric contraction before aortic ejection starts.

questions.stem: An increase in protein concentration in the interstitial fluid would tend to cause all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: an increase in interstitial oncotic pressure

options.label: E
options.text: a decrease in net transcapillary oncotic pressure gradient

questions.why: In the classical Starling model, raising interstitial protein raises its oncotic pressure and favours filtration. The revised model distinguishes bulk interstitial protein from conditions beneath the endothelial glycocalyx.

notes.A: Additional filtered fluid can raise interstitial pressure and increase lymphatic drainage while lymphatic transport capacity remains available.
notes.B: Protein raises the colloid osmotic pressure of interstitial fluid through its osmotic effect across a protein-restricting barrier.
notes.D: If lymphatic return cannot clear the extra filtered fluid, interstitial volume increases and oedema can develop.
notes.E: A rise in interstitial oncotic pressure narrows the plasma-to-interstitium difference in the classical model if plasma protein is unchanged.

questions.stem: When comparing the right ventricle to the left ventricle, all of the following are true for the left ventricle EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: muscle mass is greater in the left ventricle

options.label: B
options.text: depolarization starts first in the left ventricle

options.label: C
options.text: pressure generated in the left ventricle is greater

options.label: D
options.text: the left ventricle does more work

options.label: E
options.text: the left ventricle starts to eject blood first

questions.why: Left ventricular electrical activation begins slightly earlier, but right ventricular ejection can start first because the pulmonary valve opens against a lower downstream arterial pressure.

notes.A: The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall to generate pressure for the systemic circulation. Its muscle mass is normally greater.
notes.B: The earliest sites of ventricular activation lie on the left endocardial surface. Right ventricular activation follows shortly.
notes.C: The left ventricle generates higher pressure to drive systemic flow. The right ventricle pumps into the lower-pressure pulmonary circuit.
notes.D: With comparable stroke volumes, the higher pressure of left ventricular ejection requires more external stroke work.

questions.stem: If the diameter of a glass tube conveying fluid is doubled, the resistance to flow will be multiplied by:
questions.why: For steady laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid tube, Poiseuille resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Doubling diameter doubles radius.

notes.A: A one-half multiplier would fit simple inverse proportionality. Tube radius has a fourth-power effect under these assumptions.
notes.C: Widening the tube lowers resistance for the same fluid and length. A multiplier greater than one reverses that change.
notes.D: Sixteenfold is the increase for halving radius. Doubling it changes resistance by the reciprocal factor.
notes.E: Resistance depends strongly on lumen size even when tube length and fluid viscosity are held constant.

questions.stem: If the pressure in a sphygmomanometer cuff is slowly released, the sound of the pulse will suddenly decline when:

options.label: D
options.text: blood flow is continuous throughout the cardiac cycle.

options.label: E
options.text: when the systolic pressure is attained

questions.why: Korotkoff sounds weaken and usually disappear as cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure. The artery remains open throughout the cycle, changing the pulse-induced tissue vibrations.

notes.A: Intermittent reopening under cuff compression accompanies the audible phase. The sounds fade as the artery remains open between pulses.
notes.B: Atrioventricular valve opening is a cardiac event. The sounds heard over the cuffed arm arise locally in and around the artery.
notes.C: The relevant pressure change is deflation of the cuff to the diastolic range, not a sudden fall in the person’s blood pressure.
notes.E: At the systolic threshold, the first tapping sounds appear as the artery begins to open transiently with each pulse.

questions.stem: To use the Fick Principle to estimate cardiac output:

options.label: A
options.text: it is sufficient to know the rate of oxygen consumption by the body and arterial and venous concentrations of oxygen.

options.label: B
options.text: it is necessary to know arterial and venous concentrations of both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

options.label: C
options.text: measurements of heart rate, cardiac oxygen consumption and coronary sinus blood oxygen concentration are needed.

options.label: D
options.text: it is necessary to estimate the relative contributions by right and left ventricles

options.label: E
options.text: it is important to know the gender of the subject

questions.why: The Fick method divides whole-body oxygen consumption by the arteriovenous oxygen content difference. The venous sample must represent mixed systemic venous return for a whole-body estimate.

notes.B: An oxygen balance uses oxygen consumption and oxygen content on the two sides. Carbon dioxide measurements are not required.
notes.C: Coronary sinus blood reflects myocardial oxygen extraction. The whole-body estimate needs systemic arterial and mixed venous oxygen contents.
notes.D: In steady circulation without a significant shunt the same net flow passes through both circuits. Separate contributions are not required.
notes.E: Sex can affect population reference values but is not a term in the oxygen mass-balance equation.

questions.stem: If a volume of blood approximately equal to one-third of the circulating volume is taken from an intact, conscious animal, an increase in heart rate will occur because:

options.label: A
options.text: the heart has a smaller volume of blood to circulate.

options.label: C
options.text: the fall in blood pressure is detected by the carotid baroreceptors and this leads to vagal withdrawal, plus increased sympathetic activity.

options.label: D
options.text: blood vessels in skeletal muscles will dilate due to increased activity in the sympathetic cholinergic dilator system.

options.label: E
options.text: efferent vagal activity remains the same

questions.why: Acute blood loss reduces venous return and can lower arterial pressure. Reduced baroreceptor firing leads to vagal withdrawal and increased sympathetic stimulation, which raise heart rate.

notes.A: The smaller volume reduces filling and stroke volume. The rise in rate is mediated by a reflex response to reduced pressure.
notes.B: Increased vagal activity would slow sinoatrial firing. Blood loss normally reduces vagal efferent activity in the compensatory reflex.
notes.D: Compensation commonly includes sympathetic vasoconstriction in less immediately essential beds. Skeletal muscle vasodilatation does not explain the tachycardia.
notes.E: Vagal activity falls in the usual compensatory response. Sympathetic activation also accelerates firing of the sinoatrial node.

questions.stem: Cardiac contractility is said to be increased when:

options.label: A
options.text: cardiac output increases without a change in heart rate or left ventricular end-diastolic pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: cardiac output increases due to an increase in heart rate.

options.label: C
options.text: cardiac output increases due to an increase in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: the force-length curve for the ventricle is shifted to the right.

questions.why: Contractility (inotropy) is the strength of contraction independent of preload and heart rate. If output rises with heart rate and LV end-diastolic pressure (a preload index) unchanged, stroke volume must have risen through stronger contraction, i.e. higher contractility.

notes.B: That is a chronotropic effect.
notes.C: That is the Frank-Starling (preload) effect.
notes.D: Increased contractility shifts the curve up and to the LEFT (more force at the same length).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not primarily a function of blood plasma?
questions.why: Most oxygen in blood is bound to haemoglobin inside erythrocytes. Only a small fraction is dissolved in plasma, which mainly carries other soluble or suspended substances.

notes.A: Many hormones circulate in plasma, either freely dissolved or bound to carrier proteins, before reaching their target tissues.
notes.B: Plasma tonicity helps maintain erythrocyte volume because water moves across the cell membrane in response to osmotic gradients.
notes.C: Chylomicrons enter the circulation after lymphatic transport from the intestine and carry dietary lipids in plasma.
notes.D: Antibodies such as immunoglobulins are plasma proteins that circulate to support immune defence after secretion by plasma cells.

questions.stem: A haematocrit of 41% means that in the sample of blood analysed

options.label: A
options.text: 41% of the sample's haemoglobin is free in the plasma

options.label: B
options.text: 41% of the total blood volume is made up of plasma

options.label: C
options.text: 41% of the total blood volume is made up of red cells

options.label: D
options.text: 41% of the formed elements in the sample are red cells

options.label: E
options.text: 41% of the plasma volume is made up of plasma proteins

questions.why: Haematocrit is the fraction of whole-blood volume occupied by red cells. A value of 41 percent means erythrocytes occupy roughly two-fifths of the sampled blood volume.

notes.A: Haemoglobin is normally contained within red cells. Haematocrit does not measure plasma-free haemoglobin or haemolysis.
notes.B: The plasma fraction occupies most of the remainder after subtracting erythrocyte volume and the small buffy coat.
notes.D: The denominator includes plasma as well as formed elements. Haematocrit is not the fraction of blood cells that are erythrocytes.
notes.E: Plasma proteins form a dissolved component of plasma. Their concentration is separate from the red-cell volume fraction.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the heart is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Contraction is initiated by a nerve impulse

options.label: B
options.text: Impulses are conducted from one muscle cell to the next

options.label: C
options.text: The heart contains a number of cells with an unstable membrane potential

options.label: D
options.text: The heart contains a number of cells with a stable membrane potential

options.label: E
options.text: The ventricles are inexcitable for most of the contraction period

questions.why: Normal cardiac excitation starts in spontaneously depolarising sinoatrial pacemaker cells. Intrinsic conduction spreads it through the heart, while autonomic nerves modify rate, conduction and contractile force.

notes.B: Gap junctions connect neighbouring myocytes and let local depolarising current pass between them.
notes.C: Pacemaker cells have spontaneous phase-four depolarisation, so their membrane potential does not remain stable between action potentials.
notes.D: Working atrial and ventricular myocytes normally have a relatively stable resting membrane potential until activated.
notes.E: The ventricular action-potential plateau prolongs the refractory period, preventing re-excitation through much of contraction.

questions.stem: The sinoatrial node is the pacemaker for the heart because the SA node

options.label: A
options.text: is the most richly innervated structure in the heart

options.label: B
options.text: is the only structure in the heart capable of generating action potentials

options.label: C
options.text: has the highest rate of automatic discharge

options.label: D
options.text: has the most stable transmembrane potential

options.label: E
options.text: is the cardiac cell least sensitive to catecholamines

questions.why: Sinoatrial pacemaker cells normally reach threshold faster than other automatic cardiac cells. Their impulses activate the heart and suppress slower latent pacemakers before those cells discharge.

notes.A: Autonomic nerves modulate sinoatrial rate. Pacemaker dominance depends on intrinsic automaticity and persists in a denervated heart.
notes.B: Other conducting cells and working myocytes also generate action potentials. Latent pacemakers can discharge if sinoatrial drive is lost.
notes.D: A pacemaker cell has a changing diastolic membrane potential that drifts toward threshold, rather than a stable resting potential.
notes.E: Catecholamines can accelerate sinoatrial firing through beta-adrenergic signalling. Low catecholamine sensitivity is not why it is the usual pacemaker.

questions.stem: An independence of the P waves and the QRS complexes of the ECG indicates

options.label: A
options.text: an early repolarization of ventricular fibers

options.label: B
options.text: a failure of the AV node to conduct

options.label: C
options.text: a depression of the sinoatrial node

options.label: D
options.text: slowing of conduction at the atrioventricular node

options.label: E
options.text: a conduction block in the left bundle branch

questions.why: When P waves and QRS complexes have no fixed relationship (AV dissociation), atrial impulses are not reaching the ventricles. This is complete (third-degree) heart block from failure of AV conduction, and the ventricles are driven by an escape pacemaker.

notes.A: Early repolarisation changes the ST segment.
notes.C: SA depression slows or removes P waves but keeps P-QRS linkage.
notes.D: Slowed AV conduction lengthens the PR interval (first-degree block) but every P is still followed by a QRS.
notes.E: LBBB widens the QRS but P-QRS linkage is kept.

questions.stem: If the end-diastolic ventricular volumes are increased (within physiologic limits)

options.label: A
options.text: the stroke volume would be increased

options.label: D
options.text: the force of cardiac contraction would be decreased

options.label: E
options.text: the output of the left ventricle would exceed that of the right

questions.why: A physiological rise in ventricular end-diastolic volume increases initial fibre length. This augments force at a given inotropic state and typically raises the volume ejected.

notes.B: At an unchanged heart rate, a higher stroke volume tends to increase cardiac output rather than decrease it.
notes.C: The finding is greater ventricular filling. Venous pressure depends on how that increase occurred and need not fall.
notes.D: Within the physiological range, increased initial fibre length augments active force through length-dependent activation.
notes.E: Both ventricles respond to filling, which helps match their outputs over time. Increased end-diastolic volumes do not establish a left-to-right output difference.

questions.stem: One of the major factors that controls the force of heart contraction is the

options.label: A
options.text: initial length (preload) of cardiac muscle fibers

options.label: B
options.text: number of intercalated disks in the cardiac muscle fibers

options.label: C
options.text: number of gap junctions between cardiac muscle fibers

options.label: D
options.text: degree of depolarization in the SA node

questions.why: Initial ventricular muscle fibre length helps determine how much force develops. Filling stretches the fibres before systole and increases their force through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

notes.B: Intercalated discs mechanically and electrically link cardiac cells. Their number is not the main beat-to-beat determinant of developed force.
notes.C: Gap junctions permit electrical coupling and coordinated activation. Changes in preload alter force without requiring an altered number of junctions.
notes.D: Sinoatrial depolarisation sets the rhythm. The force of working myocardial contraction also depends on initial fibre length.
notes.E: The His bundle conducts impulses toward the ventricles. Its length does not supply the preload-dependent force adjustment.

questions.stem: Positive inotropism refers to

options.label: B
options.text: movement of blood elements related to a change in chemical gradient

questions.why: Positive inotropy means increased myocardial contractility. At a given initial fibre length and comparable loading conditions, the ventricle can develop more force or eject more effectively.

notes.A: Stroke volume can change with preload and afterload. A decrease in volume is not the definition of positive inotropy.
notes.B: Movement along a chemical gradient concerns transport or diffusion. Inotropy describes myocardial contractile strength.
notes.C: Repolarisation is the electrical recovery of pacemaker cells. It does not define a change in ventricular contractility.
notes.E: End-diastolic volume is an index of ventricular filling. Positive inotropy is defined independently of that initial filling.

questions.stem: Increased pressure within the carotid sinus causes all of the following except

options.label: A
options.text: a decrease in sympathetic tone to arterioles

questions.why: Higher carotid sinus pressure increases baroreceptor firing. The reflex decreases sympathetic vasoconstrictor activity and raises cardiac vagal activity, producing vasodilatation and slowing the heart.

notes.A: Baroreceptor input inhibits sympathetic outflow to resistance vessels. Their smooth muscle relaxes because less adrenergic drive is present.
notes.B: Reduced vascular resistance and slower cardiac rate can lower systemic arterial pressure, including pressure in the aorta.
notes.C: Increased vagal activity slows the sinoatrial pacemaker and produces reflex bradycardia.
notes.D: Withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone causes arteriolar dilatation and lowers systemic vascular resistance.

questions.stem: The effect of parasympathetic nervous stimulation on the heart is

options.label: B
options.text: increased activity of the SA node

options.label: C
options.text: increased activity of the AV node

questions.why: Vagal acetylcholine activates cardiac muscarinic receptors and slows sinoatrial pacemaker depolarisation. It also slows conduction through the atrioventricular node, helping reduce the heart rate.

notes.B: Parasympathetic input decreases sinoatrial firing rather than accelerating it. Acetylcholine increases potassium conductance and reduces pacemaker cyclic AMP.
notes.C: The atrioventricular node conducts more slowly under vagal stimulation and may transmit fewer impulses if stimulation is strong.
notes.D: Vagal stimulation does not give a general increase in contractile force. It can reduce atrial contraction, with less direct ventricular effect.
notes.E: Slowing of the heart is the expected response. The listed increases in nodal activity and force do not accompany normal vagal stimulation.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms is most important for maintaining an increased blood flow to skeletal muscle during exercise?

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in a-mediated adrenergic impulses

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in b-mediated adrenergic impulses

options.label: D
options.text: A vasoconstriction in the splanchnic and renal areas

options.label: E
options.text: A local vasodilatation secondary to the effect of local metabolites

questions.why: Contracting skeletal muscle generates local signals that relax its resistance vessels. The resulting active hyperaemia increases perfusion in proportion to demand despite heightened systemic sympathetic activity.

notes.A: A higher pressure can contribute to flow, but local reduction in resistance is the main determinant of increased perfusion of active fibres.
notes.B: Alpha-adrenergic stimulation generally increases vascular smooth muscle tone. Local metabolic signals can attenuate its effect in active muscle.
notes.C: Beta-adrenergic effects can influence perfusion. Locally generated signals best explain matching of flow to the muscles actually contracting.
notes.D: Splanchnic and renal vasoconstriction can redistribute cardiac output. It does not directly lower resistance in the exercising muscle bed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most important to blood flow regulation at the tissue level?

options.label: B
options.text: Metabolic activity of the organ or tissue

questions.why: In many organs local blood flow adapts to metabolic activity. Increased substrate use and changes in interstitial signals relax resistance vessels and raise tissue perfusion.

notes.A: Transmural pressure can trigger a myogenic response and help stabilise flow. Metabolic control matches delivery to the tissue’s demand.
notes.C: Local transmitter release can affect vessel tone, but metabolic vasodilator signals provide a major link between cellular activity and perfusion.
notes.D: Circulating mediators can alter overall vascular tone. They do not usually provide the most precise feedback for an individual active tissue.
notes.E: Cardiac output is the total systemic flow. Local arteriolar resistance helps determine the proportion reaching a particular organ.

questions.stem: Which of the following events is represented on the EKG?
questions.why: The surface electrocardiographic P wave represents summed atrial myocardial depolarisation. Small structures of the specialised conduction system ordinarily have signals too weak to appear separately.

notes.A: Sinoatrial depolarisation initiates the beat, but the small pacemaker tissue does not produce its own distinct surface deflection.
notes.B: Atrioventricular nodal conduction contributes to the PR interval. Nodal depolarisation itself is not displayed as a distinct wave.
notes.C: His-bundle signals can be measured with intracardiac electrodes. Ordinary surface ECG does not show a distinct His depolarisation wave.
notes.D: Bachmann’s bundle helps spread excitation between the atria. Its activity contributes to atrial activation without a separate visible surface wave.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: A decrease in heart rate, with stroke volume and peripheral resistance held constant, will cause a decrease in all of the following, except
questions.why: With stroke volume and arterial compliance constant, pulse pressure (roughly stroke volume / compliance) stays about the same, so it is the exception. A slower rate lowers cardiac output (HR x SV), which lowers mean arterial pressure (CO x TPR). The whole pressure wave shifts down, so systolic and diastolic pressures both fall, and diastolic falls further with the longer diastolic run-off.

notes.A: This falls along with mean pressure; pulse pressure is the one that stays about the same.
notes.B: This falls along with mean pressure; pulse pressure is the one that stays about the same.
notes.C: This falls along with mean pressure; pulse pressure is the one that stays about the same.
notes.E: This falls along with mean pressure; pulse pressure is the one that stays about the same.

questions.stem: An EKG is recorded with displays no P waves, but a normal appearing QRS and T wave. The pacemaker most likely is located in the
questions.why: No P waves with normal, narrow QRS complexes means the ventricles are activated normally through the His-Purkinje system from above, but the atria are not driving them. This is a junctional (AV nodal) rhythm, usually at 40-60 beats/min; retrograde P waves may be hidden in the QRS.

notes.A: SA node rhythm produces visible P waves.
notes.C: A His bundle focus is possible but less common.
notes.D: Purkinje or ventricular foci produce wide, bizarre QRS complexes.
notes.E: Purkinje or ventricular foci produce wide, bizarre QRS complexes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes conditions consistent with increased contractility?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased cardiac output for a given end-systolic volume

options.label: B
options.text: Increased cardiac output for a given end-diastolic volume

options.label: C
options.text: Decreased cardiac output for a given end-systolic volume

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased cardiac output for a given end-diastolic volume

options.label: E
options.text: The ventricles are inexcitable for most of the contraction period

questions.why: At matched heart rate and afterload, a more contractile ventricle ejects more from the same end-diastolic volume. A higher output at comparable filling therefore supports increased inotropy.

notes.A: An end-systolic volume alone does not control for starting volume or heart rate. Comparison should begin at comparable end-diastolic filling.
notes.C: Lower output at a given residual volume does not support enhanced ejection. Initial filling and heart rate may also differ.
notes.D: At the same filling, lower output tends to indicate poorer pumping if rate and afterload are held constant.
notes.E: Ventricular refractoriness reflects action-potential timing. It does not identify an increase in contractile performance.

questions.stem: The ventricles are depolarized or depolarizing during all of the following waves except
questions.why: The PR interval covers atrial activation and conduction toward the ventricles before the QRS complex. The QRS, ST and QT portions all include ventricular activation or its aftermath.

notes.A: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation, with activation travelling through the ventricular myocardium.
notes.B: The QT interval runs from the onset of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave and includes depolarisation and repolarisation.
notes.C: During the ST segment most ventricular myocardium remains depolarised, with little net voltage gradient across it.

questions.stem: The tendency to form edema will be increased by
questions.why: Raised venous pressure is transmitted upstream to capillaries, increasing the pressure that drives filtration. Oedema can develop when excess filtration exceeds the capacity for lymphatic return.

notes.A: Arteriolar constriction decreases downstream capillary pressure and usually limits the hydrostatic drive to filtration.
notes.C: An increase in plasma proteins raises intravascular oncotic pressure, which tends to oppose filtration across the microvascular barrier.
notes.D: Dehydration usually lowers vascular volume and can concentrate plasma proteins. Those changes do not generally favour hydrostatic oedema.

questions.stem: Myocardial contractility is best correlated with the intracellular concentration of
questions.why: The systolic rise in cytosolic calcium activates cardiac myofilaments by binding to troponin. A greater calcium transient usually increases developed force at a given muscle length.

notes.A: Intracellular sodium influences calcium handling through the sodium–calcium exchanger. Calcium is the immediate activating ion for contraction.
notes.B: Potassium contributes to membrane potential and repolarisation. It does not directly activate cardiac myofilaments.
notes.D: Chloride contributes to some membrane currents and cell volume regulation. It is not the principal link to contractile force.
notes.E: Magnesium supports enzyme and ATP functions. It does not substitute for calcium binding to troponin during activation.

questions.stem: Cardiac output of the right heart is what percentage of the left heart?
questions.why: The pulmonary and systemic circuits operate in series. Over time right and left ventricular outputs are approximately equal, otherwise blood would accumulate in one circuit.

notes.A: With a persistent output of one-quarter of left ventricular flow, the pulmonary circuit would lose blood faster than it receives it.
notes.B: A sustained one-half ratio is incompatible with steady volumes in circuits that receive and pass on the same blood.
notes.C: A transient mismatch can occur during breathing or posture changes. It cannot be sustained at a three-quarter ratio.
notes.E: A persistent right-sided output greater than left-sided output would congest the pulmonary circuit rather than maintain steady flow.

questions.stem: The reflex organization of the cardiovascular system is designed to principally maintain
questions.why: Rapid cardiovascular reflexes chiefly defend arterial pressure by adjusting heart rate, cardiac contractility and vascular tone. These adjustments preserve perfusion despite changes in posture or circulating volume.

notes.A: Local metabolic control helps match oxygen delivery to tissue need. The arterial baroreflex directly senses vessel stretch related to pressure.
notes.B: Resistance can vary widely because arterioles are effectors of cardiovascular reflexes rather than a fixed target.
notes.D: Cardiac output changes with demand and contributes to regulation. Reflex regulation does not require that output stay constant.

questions.stem: The physiological function of the relatively slow conduction through the AV node is to allow sufficient time for

options.label: A
options.text: run-off of blood from the aorta to the arterioles

questions.why: Slow conduction through the atrioventricular node delays ventricular activation after the atria depolarise. This gives atrial contraction time to finish contributing to ventricular filling.

notes.A: Aortic runoff is driven by the arterial pressure gradient during diastole. It is not the primary purpose of the nodal delay.
notes.B: Systemic and pulmonary venous return reach the atria during much of the cycle. The delay specifically allows atria to empty into ventricles.
notes.D: Ventricular contraction follows transmission of the impulse beyond the node. The delay postpones contraction so filling can finish first.
notes.E: Ventricular repolarisation occurs after ventricular activation, well after the atrioventricular delay has ended.

questions.subtopic: AV nodal delay and heart block

questions.stem: Which one of the following is the best index of preload?
questions.why: Preload reflects ventricular muscle stretch before contraction. Left ventricular end-diastolic volume is a useful estimate because it reflects chamber filling more directly than upstream pressure measurements.

notes.A: Total blood volume influences venous return but does not specify the volume or stretch in a particular ventricle.
notes.B: Central venous pressure is a right-sided filling pressure. It does not directly measure left ventricular end-diastolic size.
notes.C: Wedge pressure approximates left atrial pressure in appropriate circumstances. It does not directly measure ventricular volume or fibre stretch.
notes.E: End-diastolic pressure depends on compliance as well as filling. The same pressure can occur at different ventricular volumes.

questions.stem: Normal splitting of the second heart sound (S2) into two components is increased during inspiration because

options.label: A
options.text: The closing of the aortic valve is delayed

options.label: B
options.text: The opening of the mitral valve is delayed

options.label: C
options.text: The closing of the pulmonic valve is delayed

options.label: D
options.text: The stroke volume of the left ventricle is increased

questions.why: Inspiration increases right-sided venous return and can prolong right ventricular ejection. The pulmonary valve closes later, widening the physiological separation between the two components of the second sound.

notes.A: Inspiration may make aortic closure slightly earlier as left ventricular filling falls. Delayed aortic closure would tend to narrow the split.
notes.B: Opening of the mitral valve begins ventricular filling. It does not produce either normal semilunar closure component of the second sound.
notes.D: Right ventricular filling rises during inspiration, while left ventricular filling can fall transiently. A rise in left stroke volume is not the main mechanism.
notes.E: Heart rate may change with breathing, but the split reflects the relative timing of aortic and pulmonary valve closure.

questions.stem: Sustained elevation of cardiac output will occur with which of the following conditions?
questions.why: Anaemia reduces the oxygen carried in each unit of blood. Lower viscosity and compensatory changes in vascular resistance and cardiac flow can produce a sustained high-output state.

notes.A: Hypertension is elevated pressure and often reflects increased vascular resistance. It does not by itself imply sustained high output.
notes.B: Aortic stenosis obstructs left ventricular ejection and can limit increases in output, especially during exercise.
notes.D: Complete heart block can leave a slow ventricular escape rhythm. The reduced rate often limits cardiac output.
notes.E: Cardiac tamponade limits diastolic filling, reducing stroke volume and usually lowering cardiac output.

questions.stem: Blood pressure increases and heart rate decreases in response to
questions.why: Markedly raised intracranial pressure can evoke the Cushing response. Sympathetic vasoconstriction raises arterial pressure to defend cerebral perfusion, and the arterial pressure rise can trigger reflex bradycardia.

notes.A: Dynamic exercise typically raises systolic pressure and heart rate together. A fall in rate is not the usual exertional response.
notes.B: Increased body temperature often produces tachycardia and increased skin flow. It does not characteristically cause hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
notes.C: Acute altitude exposure often increases sympathetic drive and heart rate as oxygen availability falls.
notes.E: Haemorrhage reduces circulating volume and usually causes tachycardia as arterial pressure or filling falls.

questions.stem: Net filtration from capillaries will increase following

options.label: A
options.text: Increased contraction of the precapillary sphincter

questions.why: Increased resistance downstream of capillaries raises pressure upstream within them. The higher capillary hydrostatic pressure increases the outward driving force for fluid filtration.

notes.A: Precapillary constriction reduces pressure in the capillary bed supplied by that vessel and generally reduces filtration there.
notes.B: Lower arterial pressure generally decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure unless compensatory changes maintain it.
notes.C: More plasma protein raises intravascular oncotic pressure and strengthens the opposing effect on outward filtration.
notes.D: Reduced hydraulic permeability lowers fluid movement for a given driving pressure. It does not by itself increase filtration.

questions.stem: The greatest percentage of blood volume is found in the
questions.why: Systemic venules and veins hold the largest fraction of blood volume at rest. Their high compliance allows considerable storage at low pressure and supports redistribution when demand changes.

notes.A: The cardiac chambers contain blood during filling and ejection. Their combined volume is much smaller than the systemic venous reservoir.
notes.B: The aorta carries high pressure and supplies major arteries. Its lumen stores only a small fraction of total blood volume.
notes.C: Arteries and arterioles distribute blood and regulate resistance. They are less compliant and contain less blood than systemic veins.
notes.D: Capillaries provide a vast exchange area. Their small luminal volumes add up to less than the venous compartment.

questions.stem: Turbulence is more likely to occur in a blood vessel if

options.label: A
options.text: The velocity of blood within the vessel increases

options.label: B
options.text: The viscosity of blood within the vessel increases

options.label: C
options.text: The diameter of the vessel decreases

options.label: D
options.text: The density of the blood decreases

options.label: E
options.text: The length of the vessel increases

questions.why: Higher flow velocity increases the Reynolds number, favouring turbulence. For a given geometry, the Reynolds number rises when inertial forces increase relative to viscous damping.

notes.B: Higher viscosity damps disturbances and lowers Reynolds number, making turbulence less likely if other variables are unchanged.
notes.C: At fixed velocity, a smaller diameter lowers Reynolds number. A real stenosis can raise local velocity, so its effects interact.
notes.D: Lower density decreases fluid inertia at a given velocity and diameter and therefore decreases Reynolds number.
notes.E: Length increases resistance in a straight tube, but it is not a term in the standard Reynolds number relation.

questions.stem: Arrhythmia is characterized by
questions.why: Arrhythmia (dysrhythmia) means any abnormal rate, rhythm or conduction pattern of the heart; the core feature in this option set is irregular rhythm.

notes.A: Rapid contraction alone is tachycardia, which may still be regular.
notes.C: Valve disorders are structural and are not arrhythmias in themselves.
notes.D: Valve disorders are structural and are not arrhythmias in themselves.
notes.E: A regular beat is normal rhythm.

questions.stem: Blood flowing through a vein tends to

options.label: C
options.text: carry oxygen to the body cells

options.label: D
options.text: flow at a faster rate than in the artery

questions.why: Flow in many peripheral veins is relatively smooth because upstream resistance dampens arterial pulsations. Venous flow can still vary with breathing, muscle contraction and proximity to the heart.

notes.A: Central venous flow can be phasic, but prominent pressure waves from ventricular ejection are characteristic of arteries.
notes.C: Most systemic veins return relatively deoxygenated blood toward the heart. They do not deliver oxygen directly to systemic capillaries.
notes.D: Velocity depends on flow and total cross-sectional area. Veins are not generally faster than corresponding arteries.
notes.E: Pressure gradients and valves normally support net flow toward the heart. Sustained bidirectional flow is not the usual pattern.

questions.stem: Pulmonary:

options.label: A
options.text: blood flow equals systemic blood flow

options.label: B
options.text: vascular resistance is similar to systemic peripheral resistance

options.label: C
options.text: vein blood has high CO2 content

options.label: D
options.text: hypertension can lead to left ventricular hypertrophy

options.label: E
options.text: veins drain into the right atrium

questions.why: Pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected in series, so their net flows are closely matched in steady state. Pulmonary vascular resistance is substantially lower than systemic resistance.

notes.B: The pulmonary circuit carries comparable flow at a much lower pressure difference, implying lower vascular resistance.
notes.C: Pulmonary venous blood has given up carbon dioxide in the lungs. It normally contains less carbon dioxide than pulmonary arterial blood.
notes.D: Pulmonary hypertension increases pressure load on the right ventricle and can cause right ventricular hypertrophy.
notes.E: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood into the left atrium. Systemic veins supply blood to the right atrium.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the primary determinant of the resting membrane potential in cardiac contractile cells?
questions.why: Resting working myocardial cells are most permeable to potassium, so membrane potential lies near the potassium equilibrium potential. Other ion permeabilities and the sodium–potassium pump help sustain it.

notes.A: Sodium permeability rises when fast sodium channels open during ventricular depolarisation. Resting sodium conductance is comparatively low.
notes.C: Calcium channels contribute to the action-potential plateau and contraction. Resting potential mainly reflects potassium conductance.
notes.D: Chloride currents can affect electrical behaviour, but they do not normally dominate the resting potential of contractile myocytes.
notes.E: The sodium–potassium pump maintains the gradients and has a small electrogenic effect. Resting potassium permeability is the immediate determinant.

questions.stem: The primary pacemaker of the heart at physiological conditions is normally the:
questions.why: The sinoatrial node usually reaches firing threshold before the heart’s other automatic tissues. Its impulses activate the atria and entrain slower pacemakers during normal sinus rhythm.

notes.B: The atrioventricular node conducts atrial impulses and can generate a slower escape rhythm if sinoatrial drive fails.
notes.C: The His bundle conducts impulses to ventricular branches. Its latent automaticity does not normally set heart rate.
notes.D: The mitral valve is a mechanical structure regulating flow. It does not generate the normal pacemaker impulse.
notes.E: Ventricular escape rhythms can occur when higher pacemakers fail. Normal impulses originate before they reach the ventricles.

questions.stem: On the electrocardiogram (ECG), the QRS complex represents:
questions.why: The QRS complex is the surface ECG expression of ventricular myocardial depolarisation. Atrial repolarisation usually occurs around the same time but is obscured by the larger signal.

notes.A: Atrial depolarisation generates the P wave, which ordinarily precedes the QRS complex.
notes.B: Atrial repolarisation may overlap the QRS complex in time. Ventricular activation is the dominant source of that complex.
notes.D: Ventricular repolarisation is represented mainly by the T wave, which follows the QRS complex.
notes.E: Atrioventricular conduction delay contributes to the PR interval and occurs before the ventricles produce the QRS complex.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: An ECG would be useful for determining a patient's:

options.label: D
options.text: blockage of conduction of electrical signals between the atria and the ventricles;

questions.why: An ECG can show whether atrial electrical activity reaches the ventricles. Comparing P waves with QRS complexes and assessing the PR interval helps identify atrioventricular conduction abnormalities.

notes.A: A murmur is a mechanical sound usually detected by auscultation. An ECG does not directly record heart sounds.
notes.B: Stroke volume is blood volume ejected per beat. It requires a haemodynamic or imaging measurement rather than electrical timing alone.
notes.C: An ECG can provide heart rate, but calculating cardiac output also requires stroke volume or an independent flow measurement.
notes.E: Atrioventricular conduction can be assessed from timing and relationships on an ECG, so a relevant use is listed.

questions.stem: Cardiac output (C.O.) is the:

options.label: A
options.text: volume of blood pumped per minute by each of the both ventricles;

options.label: B
options.text: volume of blood flowing through the systemic circulation each minute;

options.label: C
options.text: product of the heart rate and the stroke volume;

questions.why: Cardiac output is the amount ejected by one ventricle per minute and equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. In steady state it approximates systemic blood flow.

notes.A: Either ventricular output can represent cardiac output in a steady circulation. The outputs are measured separately rather than added.
notes.B: Systemic flow per minute is what the left ventricle supplies in steady state, so this is another expression of cardiac output.
notes.C: Multiplying beats per minute by volume per beat gives volume per minute, the units of cardiac output.
notes.D: Ventricular flow and the rate–stroke volume relation are valid. The selection omits the equivalent steady-state systemic flow description.

questions.stem: According to the Frank-Starling mechanism of the heart:

options.label: A
options.text: with each systole the left ventricle ejects a larger volume of blood then the right ventricle;

options.label: B
options.text: the intrinsic rate of the heart's pacemaker is 100 beats per minute;

options.label: C
options.text: cardiac output increases with increased heart rate;

options.label: D
options.text: stroke volume increases with the increase of the venous return;

questions.why: Increased venous return raises ventricular filling and stretches myocardial fibres. Within physiological limits, the resulting increase in force raises stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

notes.A: Both ventricles generally eject comparable volumes over time. The mechanism helps match output to filling rather than giving the left ventricle a persistent excess.
notes.B: Intrinsic pacemaker rate is a property of automatic cells. The Starling mechanism concerns ventricular filling and ejection.
notes.C: Heart rate is a factor in cardiac output. The specific Starling response links initial fibre length to stroke volume.
notes.E: The timing of ventricular contraction reflects the conduction system. The Starling relation addresses mechanical force and output.

questions.stem: Within protodiastole of the ventricles:

options.label: A
options.text: A-V valves are opened, S-L valves closed;

options.label: B
options.text: A-V and S-L valves are closed;

options.label: C
options.text: A-V and S-L valves are opened;

options.label: D
options.text: A-V valves are closed, S-L valves are closing;

options.label: E
options.text: none of the upper mentioned is correct.

questions.why: Protodiastole refers to the short transition from late ejection to semilunar valve closure as ventricular pressure falls. Atrioventricular valves remain closed until ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.

notes.A: Open atrioventricular valves indicate the subsequent filling phase. They remain shut at the end of ventricular ejection.
notes.B: Both sets are closed during isovolumetric relaxation after semilunar closure. Protodiastole includes the transition toward that closure.
notes.C: Atrioventricular valves are closed before ejection ends. The semilunar valves are moving toward closure rather than both sets remaining open.
notes.E: There is a valid description in which the semilunar valves close while atrioventricular valves are still closed.

questions.stem: During exercise, there is an increased flow of blood to:
questions.why: In exercise, blood flow to working muscles rises many-fold through metabolic vasodilation.

notes.A: Brain flow stays almost constant because of cerebral autoregulation.
notes.B: Renal (and splanchnic) flow falls due to sympathetic vasoconstriction, freeing cardiac output for muscle.
notes.D: These include brain and kidneys, which do not increase.
notes.E: These include brain and kidneys, which do not increase.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric contraction:

options.label: A
options.text: A-V valves are opened, S-L valves are opened;

options.label: B
options.text: A-V valves are closed, S-L valves are opened;

options.label: C
options.text: A-V valves are opened, S-L valves are closed;

options.label: D
options.text: A-V valves are closed, S-L valves are closed;

questions.why: Isovolumetric contraction starts after atrioventricular valves close and ends when semilunar valves open. Both sets are closed between those events, so ventricular pressure rises at constant volume.

notes.A: Open inflow and outflow valves would allow chamber volume to change. Neither set is open during normal isovolumetric contraction.
notes.B: Closed atrioventricular valves with open semilunar valves indicate ejection, when ventricular volume decreases.
notes.C: Open atrioventricular valves with closed semilunar valves characterise ventricular filling, when the ventricles gain volume.
notes.E: Both sets are closed during the pressure rise before ejection. That configuration is represented among the choices.

questions.stem: The aortic valve:

options.label: A
options.text: prevents the backflow of blood into the aorta during ventricular diastole;

options.label: B
