options.text: prevents the backflow of blood to the left ventricle during the ventricular diastole;

options.label: C
options.text: prevents the backflow of blood into the left ventricle during ventricular ejection;

options.label: D
options.text: prevents the backflow of blood into the aorta during ejection;

options.label: E
options.text: closes when the first heart sound is heard.

questions.why: The aortic valve closes when left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure at the end of ejection. Its closed leaflets prevent aortic blood returning to the ventricle.

notes.A: During diastole the higher pressure is in the aorta. The valve prevents flow out of the aorta back toward the ventricle.
notes.C: During forward ejection the valve is open and ventricular pressure drives flow into the aorta. The backflow-preventing closure occurs later.
notes.D: Ejection is forward flow into the aorta. The valve does not block that normal direction when the ventricle is ejecting.
notes.E: Aortic valve closure supplies one component of the second sound. The first sound is associated with atrioventricular valve closure.

questions.stem: In humans, blood loss causes:

options.label: B
options.text: decreased blood flow to the skin;

options.label: C
options.text: a fall in the cardiac output;

questions.why: After haemorrhage, falling venous return lowers cardiac output (C). Baroreceptor-driven sympathetic activity constricts veins to mobilise stored blood (A) and constricts skin vessels, causing pallor and coldness (B). So E (a, b and c) is the best answer.

notes.D: Splenic contraction is an important reservoir response in animals such as dogs and horses but contributes little in humans.

questions.stem: The heart sounds:

options.label: A
options.text: express the arterial wall fluctuations synchronous with the cardiac performance;

options.label: B
options.text: register the cardiomyocytes' bioelectrical activity during the cardiac cycle;

options.label: C
options.text: reflect the volume of blood, which the heart ejects in the large and small circle per minute;

options.label: D
options.text: are registered and analysed via auscultation and phonocardiography;

questions.why: Heart sounds are mechanical vibrations associated with cardiac events such as valve closure. A stethoscope allows auscultation, while phonocardiography records the acoustic signal for analysis.

notes.A: Arterial wall fluctuations produce the arterial pulse and can be timed alongside heart sounds. They are not the cardiac sounds themselves.
notes.B: Bioelectrical activity is recorded by electrocardiography. Heart sounds reflect mechanical vibration during the cardiac cycle.
notes.C: Blood flow per minute defines cardiac output and requires a flow estimate. Acoustic timing alone does not measure it.
notes.E: Phlebography evaluates veins or, in older terminology, venous pulsations. Heart sound waveforms are recorded by phonocardiography.

questions.stem: Which of the following organs has the greatest blood flow per 100 g of tissue?
questions.why: At rest the kidneys receive a large fraction of cardiac output relative to their small mass. This produces the highest perfusion per 100 grams among the listed tissues.

notes.A: The brain has continuous perfusion to support metabolism. Its resting flow per 100 grams is substantially below renal perfusion.
notes.B: The myocardium has high oxygen extraction and a rich blood supply. Resting flow per mass is still below that of the kidneys.
notes.C: Skin flow varies with temperature and autonomic tone. Typical resting perfusion per 100 grams is lower than renal perfusion.
notes.D: The liver receives substantial total blood flow through two routes. Dividing this by its larger mass gives lower flow per 100 grams.

questions.stem: If the heart rate is 70 bt∙min-1 and the stroke volume is 75 ml, cardiac output is closest to:
questions.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Seventy beats per minute times 75 millilitres per beat gives 5,250 millilitres, or 5.25 litres, per minute.

notes.A: The specified heart rate and stroke volume yield more than this. Multiplying them gives 5,250 millilitres per minute.
notes.B: A flow of 4.55 litres per minute at 70 beats per minute would require a smaller stroke volume of 65 millilitres.
notes.D: A cardiac output of eight litres per minute would require more than 110 millilitres per beat at the given rate.
notes.E: Nearly ten litres per minute would require about 140 millilitres per beat at 70 beats per minute, above the given volume.

questions.stem: Which of ECG elements reflects the ventricular depolarisation?
questions.why: The QRS complex reflects rapid depolarisation of ventricular myocardium. The impulse spreads through the His–Purkinje system and then through ventricular muscle, generating the recorded deflection.

notes.A: The PQ or PR interval extends from the start of atrial depolarisation to the start of ventricular activation.
notes.C: The QT interval includes ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. The QRS complex is the component representing activation alone.
notes.D: The ST segment follows the QRS and corresponds to a period when much of the ventricular myocardium is already depolarised.
notes.E: The T wave is the principal surface expression of ventricular repolarisation after the QRS complex.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Cardiac output (C.O.) of the right heart is what percentage of that of the left?
questions.why: The right and left ventricles supply two circulations connected in series. Their mean outputs are approximately equal in steady state, although small transient differences can occur.

notes.A: A sustained right output of only one-quarter of left output would quickly deplete the pulmonary vascular compartment.
notes.B: One-half would represent an ongoing imbalance, causing blood to accumulate on the systemic side rather than circulate steadily.
notes.C: Brief beat-to-beat mismatches can occur with breathing. A persistent three-quarter ratio is incompatible with stable circuit volumes.
notes.E: A prolonged excess of right over left output would raise pulmonary blood volume rather than maintain steady state.

questions.stem: During the ventricular filling:

options.label: A
options.text: A-V valves are opened, S-L valves are opened;

options.label: B
options.text: A-V valves are closed, S-L valves are opened;

options.label: C
options.text: A-V valves are opened, S-L valves are closed;

options.label: D
options.text: A-V valves are closed, S-L valves are closed;

questions.why: Ventricular filling occurs when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and opens the atrioventricular valves. The semilunar valves remain closed because arterial pressure exceeds relaxing ventricular pressure.

notes.A: Open semilunar valves would connect the ventricles to the arteries. The outflow valves remain closed during normal filling.
notes.B: Closed atrioventricular valves and open semilunar valves characterise ventricular ejection, which decreases ventricular volume.
notes.D: Both sets are closed during isovolumetric phases. Ventricular volume is then constant because no inflow valve is open.
notes.E: The normal filling configuration is represented among the options. Inflow valves are open and outflow valves are closed.

questions.stem: Which effect/s is/are caused by sympathetic stimulation?
questions.why: Cardiac sympathetic stimulation increases contractile force and speeds conduction, especially through the atrioventricular node. The rise in cardiac work also increases myocardial energy and oxygen demand.

notes.A: Beta-1 stimulation increases intracellular calcium availability and can strengthen myocardial contraction at a given initial length.
notes.B: A faster, more forceful heart performs more work and consumes more oxygen. Cardiac metabolic demand therefore rises.
notes.C: Sympathetic stimulation increases atrioventricular nodal conduction velocity, shortening the delay between atrial and ventricular activation.
notes.D: The usual cardiac adrenergic response does not decrease excitability. It increases pacemaker activity and can facilitate conduction.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the ventricular myocyte action potential from that of a skeletal muscle fibre?

options.label: A
options.text: a short duration of about 0.01 s with rapid repolarisation;

options.label: B
options.text: a resting potential close to 0 mV with slow depolarisation;

options.label: C
options.text: an upstroke carried mainly by Ca2+ rather than Na+ entry;

options.label: D
options.text: a long duration of about 0.3 s with a sustained plateau;

options.label: E
options.text: an absent refractory period that allows summation.

questions.why: Ventricular myocytes have a long action potential with a plateau sustained in part by inward calcium current. The plateau lengthens refractoriness and prevents summation of contractions.

notes.A: Skeletal muscle action potentials last only a few milliseconds. Ventricular myocyte repolarisation is delayed by the plateau.
notes.B: Ventricular cells have a strongly negative resting potential. Their normal phase-zero upstroke is rapid, rather than a slow drift from zero.
notes.C: The ventricular upstroke is driven mainly by fast sodium influx. Calcium contributes strongly to the later plateau and to nodal upstrokes.
notes.E: Ventricular myocardium has a long refractory period. This limits re-excitation and prevents normal tetanic summation.

questions.stem: The integral of the values of blood pressure during one cardiac cycle is defined as:

options.label: E
options.text: closer in value to the systolic blood pressure.

questions.why: Mean arterial pressure is the time-weighted average (integral) of pressure over one cardiac cycle. It is the pressure that drives flow and is about diastolic + one third of pulse pressure.

notes.A: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic.
notes.B: Systolic and diastolic pressures are the peak and trough, not the average.
notes.C: Systolic and diastolic pressures are the peak and trough, not the average.
notes.E: Because diastole is longer, MAP is closer to diastolic than systolic pressure.

questions.stem: The duration of the cardiac cycle depends on:

options.label: B
options.text: the time needed one systole to occur;

options.label: C
options.text: the time needed one diastole to occur;

questions.why: Heart rate counts cycles per minute, so cycle duration is its reciprocal after conversion to seconds. A faster rate shortens the cycle, reducing diastole especially.

notes.A: Stroke volume measures blood ejected per beat. It does not directly set the time between successive beats.
notes.B: Systole is only part of the cycle. The time from one beat to the next also includes diastole.
notes.C: Diastole is the filling and relaxation portion. Total cycle duration includes both ventricular relaxation and contraction.
notes.E: The cardiac pause describes a period within the cycle. Beat frequency determines the time available for the complete cycle.

questions.stem: A characteristic ECG finding in hypokalaemia is:

options.label: B
options.text: a prominent U wave after the T wave;

questions.why: Hypokalaemia alters ventricular repolarisation and can produce prominent U waves following flattened T waves. The U wave can merge with the T wave and distort interval measurement.

notes.A: A shortened PR interval is not characteristic. Significant hypokalaemia can slow conduction and sometimes prolong PR.
notes.C: ST depression is more typical than ST elevation in hypokalaemia, often alongside T-wave flattening.
notes.D: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia. A flatter T wave and prominent U wave favour hypokalaemia.
notes.E: T and U waves can merge, giving apparent QT or QU prolongation. A shortened QT is not the typical finding here.

questions.stem: The earliest ECG change usually seen in hyperkalaemia is:

options.label: B
options.text: prominent U waves after the T wave;

options.label: D
options.text: ST depression with flattened T waves;

questions.why: An early recognised ECG effect of hyperkalaemia is a narrow, peaked T wave caused by altered ventricular repolarisation. ECG findings vary and may be absent despite elevated potassium.

notes.B: Prominent U waves more strongly suggest hypokalaemia, particularly when the preceding T waves are flattened.
notes.C: Early hyperkalaemia can shorten ventricular repolarisation. With more severe toxicity, conduction abnormalities such as QRS widening become prominent.
notes.D: ST depression and flattened T waves are more typical of low potassium in this comparison.
notes.E: More advanced hyperkalaemia can prolong the PR interval and attenuate P waves. A shortened PR is not the characteristic early change.

questions.stem: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume is:
questions.why: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume is the amount of blood present just before systole. A value around 100 to 130 millilitres is a common adult teaching estimate.

notes.A: A total end-diastolic volume of 10 to 30 millilitres is much lower than typical adult filling values.
notes.B: Thirty to fifty millilitres is closer to the residual amount that can remain at end-systole in many adults.
notes.C: Fifty to seventy millilitres is a common range for stroke volume, which is the amount ejected rather than the whole filled chamber volume.
notes.D: Smaller adults can have volumes within this range. The conventional unindexed teaching example of a filled ventricle is nearer 120 millilitres.

questions.stem: The automatic activity of 20-40 imp.∙min-1 is typical for the:

options.label: E
options.text: the left and right ventricular branches.

questions.why: Distal His–Purkinje tissue can generate a slow ventricular escape rhythm when higher pacemakers fail. Intrinsic rates of about 20 to 40 impulses per minute are taught for Purkinje cells.

notes.A: Proximal His tissue is part of the atrioventricular junctional system. Its typical escape rate is higher than the distal ventricular range.
notes.B: The atrioventricular junctional escape rate is usually around 40 to 60 impulses per minute.
notes.C: The sinoatrial node has the highest normal intrinsic firing rate and usually dominates the slower distal pacemakers.
notes.E: The bundle branches mainly distribute the impulse. A slow distal automatic rate is classically assigned to the Purkinje network.

questions.stem: The end diastolic volume:

options.label: B
options.text: is directly proportional to the venous return to the heart;

options.label: C
options.text: doesn't depend on length and strength, developed by the ventricular myocardium;

options.label: D
options.text: increases when the blood pressure in aorta increases;

options.label: E
options.text: doesn't depend on atrial systole and diastole.

questions.why: End-diastolic volume is set mainly by how much blood returns to the heart during diastole, so more venous return gives a higher EDV (preload).

notes.A: Stroke volume depends on EDV, not the other way round.
notes.C: Residual volume after the previous contraction (end-systolic volume) does contribute.
notes.D: Higher aortic pressure raises afterload; EDV may rise only secondarily.
notes.E: Atrial systole contributes about 20-30% of filling.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is not a vasoconstrictor:
questions.why: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released when the atria stretch. It promotes renal sodium excretion and can relax vascular smooth muscle, helping counter increased circulating volume.

notes.A: Noradrenaline stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors on many resistance vessels, producing vasoconstriction in those beds.
notes.B: Vasopressin can constrict vessels through vascular V1 receptors, in addition to its renal water-conserving action.
notes.C: Serotonin can constrict certain vessels, including through smooth muscle serotonin receptors. The effect can vary by vascular bed and endothelium.
notes.D: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor that acts on vascular smooth muscle and helps raise arterial pressure.

questions.stem: The slowest conduction (velocity) is characteristic for:
questions.why: Conduction is slowest in the atrioventricular node. Its cellular properties create a delay between atrial and ventricular activation, leaving time for atrial emptying before ventricular contraction.

notes.A: Activation passes from the sinoatrial region through atrial myocardium faster than through the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: The His bundle rapidly carries excitation from the atrioventricular junction toward the bundle branches.
notes.D: Purkinje fibres have particularly fast conduction, helping activate widely separated regions of the ventricles nearly together.
notes.E: Working ventricular muscle conducts more slowly than Purkinje fibres, but the specialised atrioventricular node supplies the principal slow segment.

questions.subtopic: AV nodal delay and heart block

questions.stem: Which of the following acts strongly on α1, β1 and β2 adrenergic receptors?
questions.why: Adrenaline activates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors, including alpha-1, beta-1 and beta-2. Its relative cardiovascular effects depend on concentration and the receptor populations present.

notes.A: Noradrenaline has strong alpha and beta-1 activity but comparatively weak beta-2 activity, so it lacks the same broad profile.
notes.C: Isoprenaline strongly activates beta-1 and beta-2 receptors. It has little alpha-1 activity.
notes.D: Phenylephrine primarily activates alpha-1 receptors and increases vascular tone. It is not a strong beta agonist.
notes.E: Dobutamine acts predominantly through beta-1 receptors, with additional effects that do not match adrenaline’s broad profile.

questions.stem: In a patient with mitral stenosis one would expect to hear:

options.label: B
options.text: a systolic murmur loudest over the base of heart;

options.label: C
options.text: a diastolic murmur, with loudest intensity over the apex of heart;

options.label: D
options.text: a diastolic murmur loudest over the base of heart;

options.label: E
options.text: systolic murmur over the apex of heart.

questions.why: A narrowed mitral valve obstructs left atrial emptying during diastole. The resulting low-pitched diastolic rumble is usually heard best at the cardiac apex.

notes.A: A continuous murmur extends across systole and diastole. Flow across the narrowed mitral valve occurs chiefly during ventricular filling.
notes.B: A systolic murmur at the base suggests an outflow lesion such as aortic stenosis. Mitral inflow is diastolic.
notes.D: A diastolic murmur at the base may reflect semilunar regurgitation. Mitral stenosis is usually best heard at the apex.
notes.E: A systolic apical murmur suggests mitral regurgitation. Stenosis produces noise during forward diastolic inflow.

questions.stem: The activity of the peripheral chemoreceptors increases when:

options.label: A
options.text: the mean arterial blood pressure is increased;

questions.why: Peripheral chemoreceptors increase their firing when arterial oxygen tension falls. Carotid bodies also respond to raised carbon dioxide and acidity, stimulating ventilation when gas exchange is inadequate.

notes.A: Higher arterial pressure activates baroreceptors. It is not the usual direct chemical stimulus to peripheral chemoreceptors.
notes.C: Lower arterial carbon dioxide generally reduces chemical drive. Increased carbon dioxide instead stimulates peripheral chemoreceptor activity.
notes.D: A decrease in hydrogen ion concentration means lower acidity. Increased acidity stimulates carotid-body activity.
notes.E: Cooling changes metabolism and ventilation, but low arterial oxygen tension is the direct chemoreceptor stimulus specified here.

questions.stem: Per 100 g of tissue, oxygen consumption at rest is highest in the:
questions.why: Resting myocardium has a high continuous requirement for aerobic ATP production. Per 100 grams it typically consumes more oxygen than the other listed tissues under resting conditions.

notes.A: The brain has a large total oxygen requirement. Per unit mass, resting myocardium generally consumes more oxygen.
notes.C: The liver has a substantial total metabolic demand. Much of that total reflects its larger organ mass.
notes.D: Kidneys receive high blood flow, but oxygen extraction is comparatively low. High perfusion does not equate to the highest consumption per mass.
notes.E: Resting skeletal muscle uses relatively little oxygen per unit mass. Consumption increases substantially during contraction.

questions.stem: The coronary blood flow is:

options.label: A
options.text: dominant in the left coronary artery in 60% of people;

options.label: B
options.text: not decreased during systole in the left ventricle better delivered to subendocardium during systole;

options.label: C
options.text: not suspended during systole in the right coronary artery;

options.label: D
options.text: better delivered to left ventricle during systole;

options.label: E
options.text: suspended during systole in the right coronary artery.

questions.why: The lower systolic pressure of the right ventricle causes less intramyocardial vascular compression. Right coronary inflow supplying the right ventricle therefore persists through more of systole.

notes.A: Anatomical dominance depends on the origin of the posterior descending artery. Right dominance is more common than left dominance.
notes.B: Left ventricular contraction compresses intramural vessels, especially subendocardially. Left coronary flow commonly falls during systole.
notes.D: Diastole is the main period of perfusion of left ventricular muscle because systolic compression has subsided.
notes.E: Right ventricular systolic compression is less intense. Right coronary flow to that region can continue during systole.

questions.stem: The second heart sound is:

options.label: A
options.text: prolonged of low frequency and strong in intensity;

options.label: B
options.text: strong, of low frequency and weak;

options.label: C
options.text: short, of high frequency and weak;

options.label: D
options.text: prolonged of high frequency and strong;

options.label: E
options.text: short, of high frequency and strong in intensity.

questions.why: S2 (closure of aortic and pulmonary valves) is shorter, higher-pitched and usually softer than S1. These semilunar valves are smaller and close sharply against high arterial pressure.

notes.A: Being longer describes S1, which is longer and lower-pitched.
notes.D: Being longer describes S1, which is longer and lower-pitched.
notes.B: 'strong' and 'weak' together is self-contradictory.
notes.E: S2 is typically softer than S1, especially at the apex.

questions.stem: If on ECG, P wave is missing, but QRS complex and T wave are normal, the pacemaker is located in:
questions.why: Absent P waves with normal QRS and T waves mean the ventricles are activated normally through the His-Purkinje system but the atria are not driving them. This is a junctional (AV nodal) rhythm at about 40-60/min; retrograde P waves may be hidden in the QRS.

notes.A: An SA pacemaker produces P waves.
notes.C: A His focus is possible but less typical.
notes.D: Purkinje or ventricular foci produce wide, abnormal QRS complexes.
notes.E: Purkinje or ventricular foci produce wide, abnormal QRS complexes.

questions.stem: The isovolumetric contraction is:

options.label: A
options.text: a part of the ejection phase of ventricular contraction;

options.label: B
options.text: a part of the contraction ventricular phase;

options.label: D
options.text: the rapid filling phase of ventricular diastole;

options.label: E
options.text: the slow filling phase of ventricular diastole.

questions.why: Isovolumetric contraction is the early pressure-building part of ventricular systole. Both inflow and outflow valves are closed, so ventricular volume cannot fall until ejection begins.

notes.A: Ejection starts when ventricular pressure opens the semilunar valves. The preceding pressure-building phase has no outflow.
notes.C: Ventricular diastole includes relaxation and filling. Isovolumetric contraction belongs to the start of systole.
notes.D: Rapid filling requires open atrioventricular valves and falling ventricular pressure. Neither condition describes early systolic contraction.
notes.E: Slow filling occurs later in diastole before atrial contraction. Ventricular pressure generation with closed valves is a separate phase.

questions.stem: The vascular baroreceptors register change in:
questions.why: Arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch are stretch receptors. They respond to the level of pressure and how quickly it changes, and the reflex mainly defends mean arterial pressure.

notes.A: Systolic and diastolic values affect firing, but the regulated variable is mean pressure.
notes.B: Systolic and diastolic values affect firing, but the regulated variable is mean pressure.
notes.C: PCO2 and pO2 are sensed by chemoreceptors.
notes.E: PCO2 and pO2 are sensed by chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: The asynchronous contraction is:

options.label: A
options.text: a phase of the ventricular systole;

options.label: B
options.text: a phase of the ventricular diastole;

options.label: C
options.text: starts with S - L valves closure;

options.label: D
options.text: ends with S - L valves opening;

questions.why: Asynchronous contraction is the early part of ventricular systole, when different ventricular regions develop tension as activation spreads. Coordinated pressure rise then leads into isovolumetric contraction.

notes.B: The ventricles are beginning to contract, so this is an early systolic event rather than a filling or relaxation phase.
notes.C: Semilunar closure occurs at the end of ejection and begins isovolumetric relaxation, much later than initial activation.
notes.D: By semilunar opening the ventricles have already completed isovolumetric pressure development and are ready to eject.
notes.E: Atrioventricular opening marks the start of filling in diastole. Early ventricular contraction occurs later.

questions.stem: The standard bipolar leads are:
questions.why: Standard bipolar limb leads I, II and III each record a voltage difference between two limb electrodes. Their orientations view the heart in the frontal plane.

notes.A: The augmented limb leads use a limb electrode compared with a composite reference, so they are conventionally called unipolar leads.
notes.C: The precordial leads use chest electrodes and a composite reference. They view activation mainly in the horizontal plane.
notes.D: The standard limb combination is valid. Adding the augmented leads would include recordings outside the standard bipolar set.
notes.E: Neither the augmented limb leads nor the precordial leads form the standard bipolar limb group.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not increased during exercise:
questions.why: In exercise, metabolic vasodilation in the large active muscle mass greatly lowers total peripheral resistance, even though vessels constrict in gut, kidney and inactive tissue.

notes.A: Stroke volume rises (more venous return and contractility).
notes.C: Systolic pressure rises.
notes.D: Heart rate rises.
notes.E: Muscle blood flow rises many-fold.

questions.stem: The peripheral baroreceptors trigger:

options.label: C
options.text: long term regulation of arterial blood pressure;

questions.why: Arterial baroreceptors adjust autonomic output in both directions. Falling pressure evokes a pressor response, while rising pressure evokes a depressor response that buffers the change.

notes.B: Reduced baroreceptor firing favours a pressor response. Increased firing activates the opposite reflex direction.
notes.C: The arterial baroreflex is especially important for rapid pressure buffering. Sustained regulation also involves renal and endocrine mechanisms.
notes.D: Increased firing produces a depressor response, but falling firing can increase sympathetic tone and evoke a pressor response.
notes.E: The Bainbridge response is associated with atrial stretch during increased venous return. The arterial pressure reflex uses separate receptors.

questions.stem: The following would directly increase the heart rate:
questions.why: Cardiac sympathetic fibres directly accelerate the sinoatrial pacemaker. Noradrenaline stimulates beta-1 receptors, increasing the rate at which pacemaker cells reach threshold between beats.

notes.B: Parasympathetic stimulation releases acetylcholine and usually slows the sinoatrial node through muscarinic signalling.
notes.C: A fall in pressure can raise heart rate through the baroreflex. The direct cardiac effector is altered autonomic input.
notes.D: Lower pressure acts indirectly through a reflex, and increased vagal stimulation tends to slow rather than accelerate the heart.
notes.E: Sympathetic input has a direct positive chronotropic effect and is included among the choices.

questions.stem: The long term regulation of arterial blood pressure is:

options.label: B
options.text: carried out by pressor and depressor baroreceptive reflexes;

options.label: C
options.text: humoral and restores the volume of blood;

options.label: D
options.text: carried out by depressor chemoreceptive reflexes;

options.label: E
options.text: carried out by ventral medial Hypothalamus.

questions.why: Longer-term arterial pressure control depends strongly on renal sodium and water balance and on hormonal signals such as the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. These alter extracellular and circulating volume.

notes.A: Neural reflexes rapidly buffer changes in pressure, but durable regulation also requires adjustment of fluid and sodium balance.
notes.B: Arterial baroreflexes can reset during sustained pressure changes. They mainly supply rapid pressor and depressor buffering.
notes.D: Chemoreceptor reflexes respond to changes in gases and acidity. They do not provide the main long-term blood-volume correction.
notes.E: The hypothalamus participates in autonomic and fluid regulation. The principal long-term mechanism here includes renal and hormonal volume control.

questions.subtopic: Determinants and long-term control of pressure

questions.stem: The physiological pacemaker of the heart is:
questions.why: The sinoatrial node generates spontaneous impulses faster than other cardiac pacemaker tissues under ordinary conditions. Its impulses initiate normal sinus rhythm and entrain downstream conducting cells.

notes.A: The atrioventricular node conducts impulses from atria to ventricles and can contribute to a slower junctional escape rhythm.
notes.B: Purkinje fibres distribute excitation in the ventricles. Their intrinsic escape rate is usually much slower than sinoatrial firing.
notes.C: The atrioventricular bundle conducts impulses into the ventricular conduction system and is ordinarily activated by the upstream pacemaker.
notes.E: The sinoatrial node is explicitly listed and normally initiates the heart’s rhythm.

questions.stem: The T wave in ECG indicates:
questions.why: The T wave reflects ventricular repolarisation. Differences in the timing of electrical recovery across the ventricular wall generate a measurable signal after the ST segment.

notes.A: Resting membrane potential is a cellular electrical state. The T wave is generated by changes during ventricular recovery.
notes.B: The P wave represents atrial depolarisation. It occurs before the ventricular QRS complex and T wave.
notes.C: Sinoatrial excitation initiates the beat, but its small signal is not separately identifiable on the routine surface ECG.
notes.E: Purkinje activation helps produce rapid ventricular excitation before the T wave. The T wave reflects recovery of ventricular myocardium.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: In a resting adult with a stroke volume of 70 ml and an ejection fraction of about 55%, the left ventricular end-diastolic volume is about:
questions.why: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume. Dividing 70 millilitres by 0.55 gives approximately 127 millilitres, closest to 130 millilitres.

notes.A: An end-diastolic volume of 50 millilitres cannot supply a stroke volume of 70 millilitres from that chamber.
notes.B: If 70 millilitres were both the filling volume and the ejected volume, the ejection fraction would be 100 percent.
notes.C: A 100-millilitre end-diastolic volume and 70-millilitre stroke volume would give an ejection fraction of 70 percent.
notes.E: With a 200-millilitre filling volume and a 70-millilitre stroke volume, the ejection fraction would be 35 percent.

questions.stem: Increased vagal tone causes:
questions.why: Greater vagal tone slows spontaneous depolarisation of sinoatrial nodal cells via muscarinic receptors. The longer interval between beats produces bradycardia and may also slow atrioventricular conduction.

notes.A: A slower rate can lower cardiac output if stroke volume is unchanged. Hypertension is not a direct effect of cardiac vagal stimulation.
notes.B: Tachycardia is an increase in heart rate. Vagal acetylcholine generally produces the opposite pacemaker response.
notes.D: Slowing of heart rate can lower output unless stroke volume changes sufficiently to compensate.
notes.E: A longer filling time could influence stroke volume indirectly. The characteristic direct effect is slowing of pacemaker discharge.

questions.stem: The dicrotic notch on aortic pressure curve is caused by the:
questions.why: The dicrotic notch appears near aortic valve closure at the end of ventricular ejection. Brief reversal of flow and elastic recoil produce a notch on the aortic pressure trace.

notes.A: Mitral closure occurs before ejection and contributes to the first heart sound. The notch follows ejection.
notes.B: Tricuspid closure is an early systolic event on the right. It does not generate the systemic arterial notch.
notes.D: Pulmonary valve closure relates to events in the pulmonary artery. The aortic notch reflects the left ventricular outflow valve.
notes.E: Atrioventricular opening occurs after isovolumetric relaxation begins. The aortic valve has already closed at the notch.

questions.stem: For the peripheral resistance of the blood flow in a definite region, of highest significance is:

options.label: C
options.text: the laminar blood flow in the vessels;

questions.why: Vessel radius has a large effect on regional vascular resistance. Under a simple laminar-flow model resistance varies with the inverse fourth power of radius, making arteriolar tone important.

notes.A: Higher viscosity increases resistance linearly in the ideal laminar-flow relationship. Radius has a fourth-power effect.
notes.B: Resistance increases with vessel length. Acute regional control mostly changes calibre rather than vessel length.
notes.C: Laminar flow is an assumption used to describe the radius–resistance relation. It is not the geometric variable the region adjusts.
notes.E: Venous valves help prevent backflow. Most rapid regional resistance changes result from altered arteriolar calibre.

questions.stem: The working myocardium:

options.label: B
options.text: is comprised of cells whose cytoplasm communicates;

options.label: C
options.text: plays the role of pacemaker of the heart;

options.label: D
options.text: is comprised of cells, connected by structures that impede the ion flow;

options.label: E
options.text: reacts to threshold stimuli with different number of excited fibers.

questions.why: Working myocardium is a functional syncytium: cells are separate but electrically coupled by gap junctions, so excitation spreads through the whole chamber and it contracts as one unit.

notes.B: The cells keep their own membranes; only ions and small molecules pass through gap junctions, with no continuous cytoplasm.
notes.C: Pacemaking belongs to specialised conducting tissue.
notes.D: The junctions ALLOW ion flow.
notes.E: The heart obeys the all-or-none law, so a threshold stimulus excites all fibres.

questions.stem: The heart rate at rest is:
questions.why: A typical resting adult sinus rate lies near 60 to 90 beats per minute. Clinical reference ranges can extend to 100, and trained individuals can have lower resting rates.

notes.A: Rates well above 100 beats per minute in a resting adult represent tachycardia unless the clinical context changes the interpretation.
notes.B: Forty to sixty is often quoted as the intrinsic junctional escape range. It can also occur with low resting sinus rates in trained adults.
notes.C: A resting rate around 50 can be physiological in some individuals. It is below the usual range intended by this question.
notes.E: Twenty to forty is more typical of a distal ventricular escape pacemaker than normal resting sinus rhythm.

questions.stem: The full compensatory pause is typical of:

options.label: B
options.text: both the atrial and the ventricular extrasystoles;

questions.why: A premature ventricular beat often leaves the sinus-node timing unchanged. The next conducted beat then occurs on the original sinus schedule, producing a full compensatory pause.

notes.A: A premature atrial impulse commonly reaches and resets the sinoatrial node. The resulting pause is usually incomplete.
notes.B: Premature ventricular and atrial beats often differ in whether sinus timing is reset, so a full pause is not typical of both.
notes.D: Atrial fibrillation has irregular ventricular timing. It does not normally provide the stable sinus cycle needed to identify a classical full pause.
notes.E: Flutter timing and atrioventricular conduction can vary. The standard full compensatory pause is described relative to sinus rhythm.

questions.stem: The rhythm of the heart is determined by:

options.label: E
options.text: the left and right bundle branches.

questions.why: Under normal conditions, the sinoatrial node discharges before other latent pacemakers and determines heart rhythm. A slower escape focus can take over if sinus impulses fail.

notes.A: The His bundle transmits impulses to the bundle branches. It is ordinarily activated by the upstream sinus impulse.
notes.B: The atrioventricular node influences conduction delay and can contribute to escape rhythm. It does not normally set sinus rhythm.
notes.D: Purkinje fibres rapidly carry ventricular impulses and can generate slow escape activity if higher pacemakers fail.
notes.E: The bundle branches distribute activation to the ventricles. In normal rhythm they follow the impulse initiated in the atria.

questions.stem: The increased heart rate is called:
questions.why: Tachycardia is a heart rate above the expected range for the setting, conventionally above 100 beats per minute in a resting adult. Its mechanism can vary.

notes.A: Tachypnoea means an increased respiratory rate. It concerns breathing rather than heart rate.
notes.B: Bradycardia refers to a low heart rate, which is the reverse of the finding asked about.
notes.C: Atrial fibrillation is a particular rhythm with disorganised atrial activity. Its ventricular rate can be fast, normal or slow.
notes.D: Atrial flutter is a specific atrial tachyarrhythmia. The general term for a fast heart rate does not specify that rhythm.

questions.stem: When the rhythm is determined by the AV node, the heart rate is:
questions.why: A junctional escape rhythm commonly runs at about 40 to 60 beats per minute. The atrioventricular junction takes over when faster impulses from the sinoatrial node stop reaching it.

notes.A: This range is typical of resting sinus rhythm. A junctional escape focus normally fires more slowly.
notes.B: Twenty to forty beats per minute is more typical of a distal ventricular escape rhythm.
notes.C: A junctional rhythm around 75 may be accelerated. It exceeds the classic range for a passive junctional escape.
notes.E: This wide range mixes several possible rates. A usual junctional escape is confined to a much narrower interval.

questions.subtopic: AV nodal delay and heart block

questions.stem: Automaticity is characteristic for:

options.label: C
options.text: conducting system cells, some neurons and smooth muscle cells;

questions.why: Automaticity is spontaneous electrical activity without an external stimulus. It occurs in cardiac pacemaker tissue and also in some spontaneously active neurons and smooth muscle cells.

notes.A: Cardiac conducting cells can fire spontaneously, but automaticity also occurs in some neuronal and smooth muscle populations.
notes.B: Typical skeletal muscle fibres require motor neuron activation. Striation does not establish whether a tissue fires spontaneously.
notes.D: Excitability is the ability to respond to a stimulus. Only some excitable cells can initiate impulses spontaneously.
notes.E: Some smooth muscle is spontaneously active, but cardiac pacemaker cells and certain neurons also show automaticity.

questions.stem: The action potential of the cardiomyocytes is characterized by:

options.label: E
options.text: period of current electrical activity, expressed as slow waves and spike potentials.

questions.why: Working myocardial cells have a rapid sodium-dependent upstroke followed by a plateau and delayed repolarisation. This long action potential differs from the shorter one in skeletal muscle.

notes.A: A slow upstroke can occur in nodal cells. Working ventricular cells depolarise rapidly and have a prolonged action potential.
notes.C: The ventricular upstroke is rapid, but the plateau makes the total repolarisation process prolonged compared with skeletal muscle.
notes.D: A slow initial upstroke is not typical of working atrial or ventricular myocardium, which has fast sodium channels.
notes.E: Slow waves plus superimposed spikes describe some smooth muscle activity. Working cardiomyocytes have a distinct plateau potential.

questions.stem: P wave of the electrocardiogram reflects:

options.label: E
options.text: the time necessary for the impulse originating in S.A. node to reach the Purkinje fibers.

questions.why: The P wave represents depolarisation spreading through right and left atrial muscle. It occurs before ventricular activation, which produces the QRS complex.

notes.A: Atrial repolarisation occurs later and is usually obscured by the much larger QRS complex.
notes.B: Ventricular depolarisation generates the QRS complex. The preceding P wave comes from atrial activation.
notes.D: The P wave reflects activation, when atrial membrane potentials become less negative. It does not represent hyperpolarisation.
notes.E: The interval up to ventricular activation includes atrioventricular and conducting-system transit. The P wave itself covers atrial depolarisation.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Asynchronous contraction of the ventricles:

options.label: A
options.text: is a phase of the ventricular systole;

options.label: B
options.text: is a phase of the ventricular diastole;

options.label: C
options.text: begins with closing the S.L. valves;

options.label: D
options.text: begins with opening the S.L. valves;

options.label: E
options.text: begins with opening the A.V. valves.

questions.why: Asynchronous ventricular contraction occurs at the start of systole as activation spreads through the ventricular muscle. Inflow and outflow valve transitions occur during later pressure changes.

notes.B: Ventricular diastole consists of relaxation and filling. Asynchronous contraction is part of early active systole.
notes.C: Semilunar valves close at the end of ejection, and isovolumetric relaxation begins with both sets of valves closed.
notes.D: Opening of semilunar valves starts ventricular ejection. Initial contraction and pressure development precede it.
notes.E: Atrioventricular valves open when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure. This occurs in diastole before the next contraction.

questions.stem: In complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block, the ECG characteristically shows:

options.label: A
options.text: a constant PR interval longer than 0.20 s on every beat;

options.label: B
options.text: progressive PR lengthening until one P wave is not conducted;

options.label: C
options.text: occasional dropped QRS complexes with a fixed PR interval;

options.label: D
options.text: absent P waves with an irregularly irregular QRS rhythm;

options.label: E
options.text: P and QRS complexes occurring independently of each other.

questions.why: In complete atrioventricular block, atrial impulses fail to conduct to the ventricles. The atria follow their own rhythm while a junctional or ventricular escape focus produces independent QRS complexes.

notes.A: A consistently prolonged PR interval with every P wave conducted describes first-degree atrioventricular delay.
notes.B: Progressive PR lengthening followed by a dropped beat characterises second-degree Mobitz type I block.
notes.C: Intermittent dropped QRS complexes with an otherwise fixed PR interval fit second-degree Mobitz type II block.
notes.D: Absent distinct P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm suggest atrial fibrillation rather than the stated pattern of complete block.

questions.stem: The stroke volume of the heart at rest is:
questions.why: Stroke volume is blood ejected by one ventricle per beat, calculated as end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. Around 70 millilitres is a typical resting adult estimate.

notes.A: Beats per minute measure heart rate. Stroke volume is measured in millilitres per beat.
notes.C: About five litres is close to a typical resting cardiac output over one minute, not the volume ejected in one beat.
notes.D: Half a litre is several times a typical resting stroke volume. The usual estimate is tens of millilitres per beat.
notes.E: Millimetres of mercury measure pressure, such as systolic arterial pressure. They are not units of volume.

questions.stem: In clinical practice, the electrical axis of the heart is determined from:

options.label: A
options.text: the net QRS deflections in the precordial (chest) leads;

options.label: B
options.text: the net QRS deflections in the standard limb leads;

options.label: C
options.text: the net P-wave deflections in the standard limb leads;

options.label: D
options.text: the net T-wave deflections in the standard limb leads;

options.label: E
options.text: the net QRS deflections in chest leads V1 and V2 only.

questions.why: The usual electrical axis is the mean frontal-plane direction of ventricular depolarisation. Net QRS deflections in limb leads, including leads I and aVF, can estimate it.

notes.A: Precordial leads view activation mainly in the horizontal plane. They are not used alone for the standard frontal QRS axis.
notes.C: P-wave deflections can define an atrial axis. The standard electrical axis here concerns ventricular depolarisation.
notes.D: T-wave deflections reflect ventricular repolarisation and can define a separate T-wave axis.
notes.E: Chest leads V1 and V2 provide local precordial information. The frontal-plane axis uses limb-lead projections.

questions.stem: The augmented unipolar leads are:

options.label: D
options.text: VI, V2, V3, V4, V5 and V6;

questions.why: The augmented limb leads aVR, aVL and aVF each compare a limb electrode with a reference formed from the other limb electrodes. They sample frontal-plane electrical activity.

notes.A: Leads I, II and III are standard bipolar limb leads. Each compares potentials between a selected pair of limbs.
notes.C: The augmented limb leads are correct, but adding the standard bipolar leads makes the group too broad.
notes.D: The chest leads are unipolar precordial leads, but ‘augmented’ identifies the three limb leads in this classification.
notes.E: The augmented set excludes the precordial chest leads, even though those also use a composite reference.

questions.stem: The auscultation of the mitral valve is performed at:

options.label: A
options.text: II-nd sternal intercostal space, right of the sternum;

options.label: B
options.text: V-th intercostal space, 2 cm medial to the midclavicular line;

options.label: C
options.text: IV-th sternal intercostal space, right of the sternum;

options.label: D
options.text: II-nd sternal intercostal space, left of the sternum;

options.label: E
options.text: III-rd sternal intercostal space, left of the sternum.

questions.why: Mitral sounds are best heard at the cardiac apex, usually in the left fifth intercostal space near the midclavicular line. The precise position varies between individuals.

notes.A: The right second intercostal space next to the sternum is the usual aortic auscultation area.
notes.C: A right parasternal fourth-space point is not the usual apical projection for mitral sounds.
notes.D: The left second intercostal space at the sternal border is the usual pulmonary auscultation area.
notes.E: The left third parasternal space is an additional listening area for some murmurs. The mitral area lies lower and more lateral.

questions.stem: The 'plateau'- phase of the cardiomyocytes' action potential is due to:

options.label: A
options.text: outflux of K+ from the cells;

options.label: B
options.text: influx of Na+ into the cells;

options.label: C
options.text: influx of K+ into the cells;

options.label: D
options.text: slow influx of Ca2+ into the cells;

options.label: E
options.text: influx of Na+ into the cells and outflow of K+ from the cells.

questions.why: The ventricular plateau is sustained by slow inward calcium current through L-type channels balanced by outward potassium current. This prolongs depolarisation and helps trigger contraction.

notes.A: Potassium efflux provides outward current during the plateau and helps repolarise the cell when inward calcium current declines.
notes.B: Fast sodium influx produces the rapid upstroke. Those channels inactivate well before the plateau ends.
notes.C: The important potassium current during the plateau is outward, which counterbalances inward movement of positively charged calcium ions.
notes.E: Outward potassium current matters, but the major sustained inward current that defines the plateau is carried by calcium.

questions.stem: The extrasystoles are:

options.label: D
options.text: extraordinary, only currently interrupting the cardiac rhythm, contractions of the cardiac muscle;

questions.why: An extrasystole is a premature cardiac beat caused by an impulse arising before the next expected beat. It can transiently interrupt the rhythm without producing sustained tachycardia.

notes.A: A sustained rate above 200 describes a tachyarrhythmia rather than the isolated premature beat asked about here.
notes.B: Conduction problems alter propagation. A premature beat is defined by early impulse generation, even if its conduction is also abnormal.
notes.C: Altered excitability, automaticity or triggered activity can produce an early impulse. The premature contraction is its mechanical consequence.
notes.D: A premature contraction interrupts the expected rhythm, which describes the event. The combination also includes the electrical disturbance.

questions.stem: The electrical axis of the heart is of indifferent type when α- angle is:
questions.why: In the classical classification of the electrical axis (alpha angle), the 'indifferent' (intermediate, normal) position is about +30 to +60 degrees.

notes.A: +60 to +90 is the vertical position.
notes.D: +30 to -30 includes the horizontal position and the start of left deviation.
notes.E: Beyond -30 is left axis deviation.
notes.C: 'from -90 upward' is not a defined normal type.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is not a vasoconstrictor:
questions.why: Kinins such as bradykinin generally promote vasodilatation through endothelial signalling, including nitric oxide and prostacyclin release. Several other listed mediators can constrict resistance vessels.

notes.A: Noradrenaline activates vascular alpha adrenergic receptors and commonly produces systemic arteriolar constriction.
notes.B: Adrenaline can cause alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, particularly at higher concentrations. Beta-2 vasodilatation can predominate in some beds.
notes.C: Serotonin can constrict some vessels through smooth muscle receptors. Its net effects depend on the vascular bed and endothelium.
notes.D: Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor in many vascular beds and helps raise systemic vascular resistance.

questions.stem: In a healthy resting adult, the diastolic arterial pressure normally lies within:
questions.why: Normal resting diastolic pressure is about 60-90 mmHg (typically about 80 mmHg).

notes.A: Below about 60 mmHg is low and may threaten coronary perfusion, which mostly occurs in diastole.
notes.C: A diastolic pressure of 95-110 mmHg indicates hypertension.
notes.D: These are systolic-range values; as diastolic pressures they would mean severe hypertension.
notes.E: These are systolic-range values; as diastolic pressures they would mean severe hypertension.

questions.stem: Which of the following doesn't affect the gradient of the blood pressure:
questions.why: A pressure gradient across a vascular bed depends on flow and resistance. Minute ventilation is not a direct term in that relation, although breathing can indirectly affect haemodynamics.

notes.A: Cardiac output supplies systemic flow. For a given vascular resistance, greater flow requires a greater pressure gradient.
notes.C: Viscosity affects resistance for a given vessel geometry. This changes the pressure drop needed to sustain a specified flow.
notes.D: Total peripheral resistance is the pressure difference across the systemic circulation divided by systemic flow.
notes.E: Circulating volume can alter venous pressure, filling and cardiac output. These changes influence the pressure gradient indirectly.

questions.subtopic: Determinants and long-term control of pressure

questions.stem: Throughout the isovolumetric relaxation of the ventricles:

options.label: A
options.text: A.V. valves are opened, S.L. valves - opened;

options.label: B
options.text: A.V. valves are closed, S.L. valves - opened;

options.label: C
options.text: A.V. valves are opened, S.L. valves - closed;

options.label: D
options.text: A.V. valves are closed, S.L. valves - closed;

questions.why: After ejection ends, semilunar valves close while atrioventricular valves remain closed. Pressure falls at constant ventricular volume until the inflow valves open and ventricular filling starts.

notes.A: If both sets were open, the ventricle could exchange blood with atria or arteries and volume would not remain fixed.
notes.B: Open semilunar valves with closed atrioventricular valves describe ventricular ejection, which precedes the relaxation interval.
notes.C: Open atrioventricular valves indicate that filling has started. This occurs after isovolumetric relaxation ends.
notes.E: The combination of closed inflow and closed outflow valves is present among the choices for this phase.

questions.stem: The first heart sound is:

options.label: A
options.text: systolic, result of the ventricular contractions;

options.label: B
options.text: systolic, result of'the A.V. valves closing;

options.label: C
options.text: systolic, result of the S.L valves closing;

options.label: D
options.text: diastolic, result of the A.V. valves closing;

questions.why: The first heart sound occurs at the beginning of ventricular systole. Rising ventricular pressure closes the atrioventricular valves and produces vibrations of the associated cardiac structures.

notes.A: The timing is correct. Ventricular contraction raises pressure and triggers closure of the atrioventricular valves, which explains the sound.
notes.B: Mitral and tricuspid closure produce the main components of the first sound. Their closure occurs at the start of systole.
notes.C: Semilunar valve closure generates the second heart sound at the end of ejection.
notes.D: The valve association is correct, but closure occurs when ventricular systole begins rather than during ventricular diastole.

questions.stem: Cardiac output (C.O.) depends on:
questions.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Stroke volume can change when preload or afterload varies.by changing how much the ventricle fills and how easily it ejects.

notes.A: Vital capacity describes an exhalable lung volume. It does not enter the equation for cardiac output.
notes.B: Stroke volume gives output per beat. It must be combined with the rate to calculate volume per minute.
notes.C: Heart rate gives beats per minute. Cardiac output also depends on how much blood each beat ejects.
notes.D: Stroke volume can change when preload or afterload varies. The direct equation for cardiac output uses stroke volume and heart rate.

questions.stem: The intracardial regulation of the heart is carried out by:

options.label: D
options.text: adaptation to changes in venous return or the change in peripheral resistance;

questions.why: Intracardiac (intrinsic) regulation is the heart's self-adjustment without nerves or hormones. It adapts to venous return through the heterometric Frank-Starling mechanism and to changes in peripheral resistance through homeometric mechanisms such as the Anrep effect.

notes.A: Reflex, neural and humoral regulation are EXTRACARDIAC.
notes.B: Reflex, neural and humoral regulation are EXTRACARDIAC.
notes.C: Reflex, neural and humoral regulation are EXTRACARDIAC.
notes.E: Automaticity generates the rhythm but does not adapt output to load.

questions.stem: The heart would stop in diastole because of:

options.label: A
options.text: increased level of Ca2+ in the extracellular fluid;

options.label: D
options.text: increased concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid (above 8 mmol.l-1);

options.label: E
options.text: increased secretion of T3 and T4.

questions.why: High extracellular K+ (above about 8 mmol/L) depolarises the resting membrane and inactivates fast Na+ channels. Excitability and conduction fail and the heart stops in a relaxed (diastolic) state; this is the principle of cardioplegia solutions.

notes.A: High Ca2+ tends to cause arrest in contraction (systole).
notes.B: Catecholamines, glucocorticoids and thyroid hormones increase rate and/or contractility.
notes.C: Catecholamines, glucocorticoids and thyroid hormones increase rate and/or contractility.
notes.E: Catecholamines, glucocorticoids and thyroid hormones increase rate and/or contractility.

questions.stem: When the heart rate is 60 bt∙min-1, the duration of the cardiac cycle is:
questions.why: Heart rate is the number of cardiac cycles per minute. At 60 beats per minute, dividing 60 seconds by 60 cycles gives one second per cycle.

notes.A: A half-second cycle would correspond to 120 beats per minute, twice the stated rate.
notes.B: A cycle lasting 0.8 seconds would give 75 beats per minute rather than 60.
notes.D: A 0.2-second cycle would require 300 cycles per minute, far above the stated heart rate.
notes.E: One second is the duration calculated from the stated rate and appears explicitly among the choices.

questions.stem: The pulse pressure is:

options.label: A
options.text: closer in value to the systolic than to the diastolic pressure;

options.label: B
options.text: mean arithmetic of systolic and diastolic pressures;

options.label: C
options.text: closer in value to the diastolic than to the systolic pressure;

options.label: D
options.text: the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressure;

options.label: E
options.text: one third of the mean arterial pressure.

questions.why: Pulse pressure is the difference between the highest arterial pressure during systole and the lowest arterial pressure during diastole. It depends on stroke volume and arterial compliance.

notes.A: Pulse pressure is a difference rather than a pressure point between systolic and diastolic readings.
notes.B: An arithmetic average combines the two pressures by addition and division. Calculating pulse pressure instead requires subtraction.
notes.C: The value measures the excursion between peak and trough. It need not be a particular distance from either absolute reading.
notes.E: The familiar one-third approximation estimates mean arterial pressure by adding part of the pulse pressure to diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: The cardiovascular center is situated in:
questions.why: Key cardiovascular control circuits lie in the medulla oblongata. They integrate afferent information and adjust autonomic output controlling heart rate, contractility and vascular tone.

notes.A: The hypothalamus influences autonomic responses during stress and temperature regulation. It modulates rather than houses the principal medullary reflex circuits.
notes.B: The mesencephalon is the midbrain. Major arterial baroreflex integration occurs farther caudally in the medulla.
notes.C: Cortical activity can affect autonomic output. The core cardiovascular reflex processing is carried out in the brainstem.
notes.E: Spinal cord segments carry sympathetic output toward the heart and vessels. Their activity is regulated by brainstem pathways.

questions.stem: In the pulmonary circulation blood leaves the:

options.label: A
options.text: right ventricle and goes directly to the aorta;

options.label: B
options.text: right ventricle and moves to the lungs;

options.label: C
options.text: right atrium and goes directly to the left ventricle;

options.label: D
options.text: right atrium and goes directly to the lungs;

options.label: E
options.text: left ventricle and moves to the lungs.

questions.why: Pulmonary circulation begins with right ventricular ejection into the pulmonary trunk and arteries. Blood reaches lung capillaries for gas exchange and returns to the left atrium.

notes.A: The right ventricle ejects into the pulmonary trunk. The aorta receives blood from the left ventricle.
notes.C: The right atrium passes blood into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve rather than directly into the left ventricle.
notes.D: The right atrium passes blood to the right ventricle. That ventricle supplies the pressure for pulmonary arterial flow.
notes.E: The left ventricle ejects into the aorta and supplies systemic circulation. The right ventricle supplies the lungs.

questions.stem: In the systemic circulation, blood leaves the:

options.label: A
options.text: left ventricle and goes directly to the aorta;

options.label: B
options.text: right ventricle and goes directly to the aorta;

options.label: C
options.text: right ventricle and moves to the lungs;

options.label: D
options.text: lungs and moves to the left atrium;

options.label: E
options.text: right atrium and goes directly to the lungs.

questions.why: Systemic circulation begins with left ventricular ejection through the aortic valve into the aorta. Systemic venous blood ultimately returns to the right atrium.

notes.B: The aorta receives blood directly from the left ventricle. Right ventricular output enters the pulmonary trunk.
notes.C: Right ventricular flow to the lungs describes pulmonary circulation rather than systemic arterial outflow.
notes.D: Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium. This completes the pulmonary circuit.
notes.E: The right atrium receives systemic venous blood and passes it into the right ventricle before it reaches the lungs.

questions.stem: The cardiac cycle includes all of the following events except:

options.label: A
options.text: the movement of impulses from the SA node to all regions of the heart wall;

options.label: B
options.text: the closing and opening of the heart valves during each heart beat;

options.label: C
options.text: the number of times the heart beats in one minute;

options.label: D
options.text: the changes in pressure gradients in all chambers of the heart;

options.label: E
options.text: the changes in blood volume in all chambers of the heart.

questions.why: The cardiac cycle consists of electrical and mechanical events within a single heartbeat. Heart rate counts how many times that cycle occurs in one minute.

notes.A: An impulse begins in the sinoatrial node and propagates through atrial, conducting and ventricular tissue during each heartbeat.
notes.B: Valve positions change as pressure gradients reverse during the cycle, directing forward flow and preventing backflow.
notes.D: Pressure rises with contraction and falls with relaxation. These changing gradients drive flow and determine when valves move.
notes.E: Chamber volumes change during filling and ejection. Ventricular volume stays constant only during the isovolumetric phases.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances is synthesised by the vascular endothelium and helps to regulate blood pressure?
questions.why: Endothelial nitric oxide synthase produces nitric oxide in blood vessels. It diffuses into nearby smooth muscle and activates cyclic GMP signalling, relaxing the vessel.

notes.A: Antidiuretic hormone is synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It has renal and vascular actions.
notes.B: Atrial natriuretic peptide is secreted mainly by stretched atrial myocytes. It is not the endothelial vasodilator in this item.
notes.C: Renin is released primarily by renal juxtaglomerular cells. Its downstream products help regulate pressure and salt balance.
notes.E: Adrenaline is released mainly by the adrenal medulla. It is a circulating hormone rather than the local endothelial mediator asked for.

questions.stem: Exchange of nutrients and gases between the blood and tissue cells is the main function of the:
questions.why: Capillaries have a thin endothelial wall and provide a large surface area for exchange. Gases and small solutes move between blood and tissues across that short barrier.

notes.A: Arterioles chiefly control local resistance and delivery to downstream exchange vessels. Their smooth muscle can change lumen calibre.
notes.B: Arteries conduct and distribute blood under pressure. Their thicker walls are not the principal site of exchange.
notes.C: Veins return blood toward the heart and serve as a compliant reservoir. Most nutrient and gas transfer occurs before blood reaches them.
notes.E: Postcapillary venules can exchange fluid and allow leukocyte passage, but capillaries provide the principal surface for nutrient and gas exchange.

questions.stem: In the heart, (within physiological limits) the strength of contraction is directly proportional to the:

options.label: C
options.text: initial length of the cardiac muscle;

questions.why: Within the physiological range of filling, an increase in initial myocardial fibre length increases active force. Length-dependent activation helps link ventricular preload to systolic performance.

notes.A: Pacemaker activity determines how often the heart beats. Initial fibre stretch has a direct effect on force at a given rate.
notes.B: The atrioventricular delay allows filling before contraction. It is timing rather than the muscle’s length–force relation.
notes.D: Breathing can influence venous return, but the immediate mechanical determinant described is initial cardiac fibre length.
notes.E: The ST segment reflects an electrical phase after ventricular depolarisation. It is not a measure of initial mechanical stretch.

questions.stem: The inferior vena cava brings blood from the lower regions of the body and empties into the:
questions.why: The inferior vena cava collects systemic venous blood from structures below the diaphragm and enters the right atrium. Blood then crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

notes.A: The left atrium receives pulmonary veins. Systemic caval return enters the opposite atrium.
notes.C: The aorta is the systemic arterial outlet from the left ventricle, not a destination for caval venous blood.
notes.D: The left ventricle is filled from the left atrium across the mitral valve. Caval flow reaches the right side first.
notes.E: Blood passes into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve. The vena cava opens into the right atrium.

questions.stem: The pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.why: The sinoatrial node has the fastest normal spontaneous firing rate and initiates sinus rhythm. Downstream conducting tissues follow its timing unless a slower escape focus takes over.

notes.A: Purkinje fibres distribute ventricular activation and have latent automaticity. They normally follow impulses arriving from higher pacemakers.
notes.B: Bundle branches conduct impulses down the septum. They do not normally initiate the heartbeat.
notes.C: The His bundle carries excitation from the atrioventricular junction to the bundle branches, downstream of sinus initiation.
notes.D: The atrioventricular node delays impulses and can take part in an escape rhythm. It ordinarily follows sinoatrial activation.

questions.stem: The tricuspid valve is located between the:
questions.why: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve. It opens for flow from the right atrium into the right ventricle and closes during ventricular systole.

notes.A: The right and left atria are separated by the interatrial septum. A normal valve does not connect them.
notes.B: The ventricles are separated by the interventricular septum. The tricuspid valve is located at the right ventricular inflow.
notes.D: The mitral valve occupies the opening from left atrium to left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is on the right.
notes.E: The right ventricular outflow leads through the pulmonary valve to the pulmonary trunk. The aorta arises from the left ventricle.

questions.stem: When the mitral valve closes, it prevents the backflow of blood from the:

options.label: A
options.text: left atrium into the left ventricle;

options.label: B
options.text: left ventricle into the left atrium;

options.label: C
options.text: right atrium into the right ventricle;

options.label: E
options.text: right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.

questions.why: Rising left ventricular pressure closes the mitral valve at the beginning of systole. The closed valve prevents reverse flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.

notes.A: The normal forward direction during filling is from the left atrium into the left ventricle, when the mitral valve is open.
notes.C: The right atrium supplies the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve. The mitral valve lies on the left side.
notes.D: Flow from left ventricle to aorta passes through the aortic valve during ejection. The mitral valve guards the inlet.
notes.E: The right ventricle ejects through the pulmonary valve. The mitral valve has no direct role at that outflow.

questions.stem: Which of the following elements of the conducting system has the slowest velocity of conduction:
questions.why: The atrioventricular node is the principal slow-conducting segment between atria and ventricles. Its delay helps the atria contract and empty before ventricular systole begins.

notes.A: The sinoatrial node initiates the impulse. The characteristic delay between atrial and ventricular activation is at the atrioventricular node.
notes.B: Activation passes through atrial myocardium more rapidly than it travels through the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: Purkinje fibres have high conduction velocity, which helps activate the large ventricular myocardium in a coordinated sequence.
notes.E: The His bundle carries excitation rapidly from the atrioventricular node toward the ventricular bundle branches.

questions.subtopic: AV nodal delay and heart block

questions.stem: The myocardium functions as a functional syncytium due to:

options.label: A
options.text: the presence of striations in the myocardium;

options.label: C
options.text: the presence of gap junctions (intercalated disks);

questions.why: Gap junction channels at intercalated discs allow ionic current to pass between adjoining myocytes. Electrical coupling coordinates activity across many separate cells as a functional syncytium.

notes.A: Striations are produced by ordered sarcomeres. They help identify the contractile apparatus but do not conduct current between cells.
notes.B: Branching describes cell shape and contact geometry. Gap junction pores supply the low-resistance electrical connections.
notes.D: Desmosomes provide strong mechanical adhesion while the heart contracts. Gap junctions provide the path for intercellular current.
notes.E: Calcium activates contraction inside each myocyte. Its concentration alone does not create electrical continuity between cells.

questions.stem: Positive bathmotropic effect on the heart is produced by:
questions.why: Bathmotropy means excitability. Sympathetic stimulation (noradrenaline at beta1 receptors) increases excitability, a positive bathmotropic effect, along with positive chrono-, ino- and dromotropic effects.

notes.A: Vagal stimulation is negatively bathmotropic.
notes.C: Atropine and vagotomy only REMOVE vagal inhibition rather than directly stimulating the heart.
notes.D: Atropine and vagotomy only REMOVE vagal inhibition rather than directly stimulating the heart.
notes.E: Raised K+ depolarises cells and inactivates Na+ channels, reducing excitability.

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricle increases during:

options.label: D
options.text: stimulation of parasympathetic nerves to the heart;

questions.why: Local vasodilator signals increase coronary flow when the myocardium is hypoxic and vascular reserve remains. Left ventricular inflow is ordinarily greatest during diastole, when compression is relieved.

notes.A: Early ventricular contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels and decreases left coronary flow, particularly near the subendocardium.
notes.C: Cooling lowers myocardial metabolic demand and generally reduces the signals that increase coronary flow.
notes.D: Parasympathetic stimulation usually slows the heart and can reduce demand. It does not reliably provide the metabolic stimulus of myocardial hypoxia.
notes.E: Atrioventricular block changes rhythm and ventricular rate. It does not consistently increase local coronary flow through metabolic vasodilatation.

questions.stem: Local metabolic activity is the main factor determining the rate of blood flow to the:
questions.why: Coronary flow closely tracks the myocardium’s oxygen demand. The heart already extracts much of the delivered oxygen, so increased work depends mainly on increasing local perfusion.

notes.B: Skin flow is strongly influenced by thermoregulation and sympathetic tone as well as local factors.
notes.C: Gland perfusion can rise with activity, but the category includes different organs. Coronary flow shows the classic close match to oxygen consumption.
notes.D: Pulmonary flow is set largely by right ventricular output. Regional distribution depends strongly on ventilation and alveolar oxygen.
notes.E: Renal perfusion is high relative to metabolic demand and is controlled substantially by myogenic and tubuloglomerular autoregulation.

questions.stem: The blood–brain barrier is formed mainly by:

options.label: A
options.text: a layer of oligodendrocyte myelin wrapped around capillaries;

options.label: B
options.text: microglial cells lining the outer surface of brain capillaries;

options.label: C
options.text: tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells;

options.label: D
options.text: ependymal cells joined by tight junctions around capillaries;

options.label: E
options.text: fenestrations sealed by a thick capillary basement membrane.

questions.why: Tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells restrict movement through intercellular spaces. These cells form the principal barrier and are supported by pericytes and nearby astrocyte endfeet.

notes.A: Oligodendrocytes form myelin around central axons. The barrier separating blood from brain interstitial fluid lies in capillary endothelium.
notes.B: Microglia are resident immune cells of the central nervous system. They do not form the endothelial seal.
notes.D: Ependyma lines ventricles. The distinct blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier is mainly at choroid plexus epithelium, rather than typical ependyma.
notes.E: Most brain capillary endothelial cells lack fenestrations. The tight junctions and selective transcellular transport form the principal barrier.

questions.stem: Compared with the first heart sound, the second heart sound is normally:

options.label: A
options.text: longer in duration and lower in pitch;

options.label: B
options.text: shorter in duration and higher in pitch;

options.label: C
options.text: produced by closure of the AV valves;

options.label: D
options.text: heard at the onset of ventricular systole;

options.label: E
options.text: loudest over the cardiac apex in health.

questions.why: The second heart sound, associated with aortic and pulmonary valve closure, is normally shorter and higher pitched than the first sound. It is often prominent at the base.

notes.A: The first sound generally has a longer, lower-pitched quality. The second is typically briefer and higher pitched.
notes.C: Atrioventricular valve closure is associated with the first sound. The second follows closure of the semilunar valves.
notes.D: The onset of ventricular systole produces the first sound. The second occurs near the end of ejection.
notes.E: The second sound is generally prominent over the base. The first sound is often more prominent over the apex.

questions.stem: Pulmonary vascular resistance is:

options.label: A
options.text: is equal to that offered by the systemic circuit;

options.label: B
options.text: decreased when alveolar oxygen pressure falls;

options.label: C
options.text: expressed in units of volume flow per unit time per unit pressure gradient;

options.label: E
options.text: regulated reflexively by sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves.

questions.why: During exercise, the pulmonary circulation accommodates greater flow by recruiting and distending vessels. These changes lower pulmonary vascular resistance despite the increase in pulmonary blood flow.

notes.A: The pulmonary pressure gradient is much smaller than the systemic gradient at comparable flow, indicating lower resistance.
notes.B: Low alveolar oxygen promotes local pulmonary vasoconstriction. This raises resistance in the affected vascular region.
notes.C: Flow divided by pressure difference is conductance. Vascular resistance is pressure difference divided by volume flow rate.
notes.E: Pulmonary vessels have autonomic innervation, but recruitment, distension and local oxygen effects are major determinants of resistance in this comparison.

questions.stem: Blood flow in which of the following vascular beds is LEAST affected by sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves?
questions.why: Cerebral blood flow is strongly controlled by local metabolism, arterial carbon dioxide and autoregulation. The cerebral circulation is comparatively less dependent on sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone under ordinary conditions.

notes.B: Splanchnic vessels have substantial sympathetic tone and constrict during haemorrhage or other states requiring redistribution.
notes.C: Renal sympathetic activation can constrict resistance vessels, lower renal blood flow and promote renin release.
notes.D: Skin circulation is strongly controlled by sympathetic pathways, particularly across changes in body temperature and sympathetic drive.
notes.E: Skeletal muscle vessels receive sympathetic vasoconstrictor input. Local signals can attenuate that effect in actively contracting muscle.

questions.stem: In the heart:

options.label: A
