options.text: the left atrial wall is about three times thicker than the right atrial wall;

options.label: B
options.text: systolic contraction normally begins in the left atrium;

options.label: C
options.text: excitation spreads directly from atrial muscle cells to ventricular muscle cells;

options.label: D
options.text: atrial and ventricular muscle contracts simultaneously in systole;

options.label: E
options.text: the contracting ventricles shorten from apex to base.

questions.why: As the ventricles contract, the base (AV valve plane) is pulled down towards the fairly fixed apex, shortening the ventricle along its long axis.

notes.A: The threefold wall difference applies to the VENTRICLES (LV vs RV); the atrial walls are similar.
notes.B: Excitation starts at the SA node in the RIGHT atrium.
notes.C: The fibrous skeleton blocks direct atrial-ventricular muscle conduction, so the only route is through the AV node and His bundle.
notes.D: Atrial systole comes before ventricular systole.

questions.stem: When measuring blood pressure by the auscultatory method:

options.label: A
options.text: the sounds that are heard are generated in the heart;

options.label: B
options.text: the cuff pressure at which the first sounds are heard indicate the systolic pressure;

options.label: C
options.text: the cuff pressure at which the loudest sounds are heard indicate diastolic pressure;

options.label: D
options.text: systolic pressure estimations tend to be lower than those made by the palpatory method;

options.label: E
options.text: wider cuffs are required for smaller arms.

questions.why: During cuff deflation the first Korotkoff sounds indicate systolic pressure. Their later disappearance usually marks diastolic pressure, and the cuff bladder is sized to arm circumference.

notes.A: The arterial pulse beneath the cuff produces local tissue vibrations. Heart sounds are generated separately in the thorax.
notes.C: Diastolic pressure usually corresponds to the disappearance of sounds. The loudest sounds do not define that threshold.
notes.D: A palpable pulse can be detected only after sufficient flow has returned. Auscultatory readings can also be affected by an unrecognised gap.
notes.E: Wider cuff bladders are needed for larger arm circumferences. An oversized cuff on a small arm can underestimate pressure.

questions.stem: The absolute refractory period of ventricular muscle:

options.label: A
options.text: is shorter than the absolute refractory period of atrial muscle;

options.label: B
options.text: coincides approximately with the period of ventricular relaxation;

options.label: C
options.text: lasts from the upstroke until about mid-way through repolarisation;

options.label: D
options.text: is the time when only a stronger-than-normal stimulus can excite;

options.label: E
options.text: lengthens markedly during parasympathetic stimulation of the heart.

questions.why: Ventricular myocardium is absolutely refractory from the start of depolarisation into repolarisation, because many fast sodium channels remain inactivated. Excitability returns gradually as those channels recover.

notes.A: Ventricular myocytes usually have a longer action potential and refractory period than atrial myocytes.
notes.B: The absolute refractory period overlaps much of ventricular contraction. It does not mainly coincide with the later relaxation phase.
notes.D: A stronger stimulus can elicit a response during relative refractoriness. Absolute refractoriness prevents re-excitation regardless of stimulus strength.
notes.E: Vagal effects are strongest in nodal and atrial tissue. Marked prolongation of ventricular absolute refractoriness is not its defining effect.

questions.stem: When the eyeballs are pressed the reflex that is triggered is called:
questions.why: The Aschner–Dagnini or oculocardiac reflex is a trigeminovagal reflex. Sensory input from ocular structures can activate vagal outflow and slow the sinoatrial pacemaker.

notes.A: Goltz’s reflex classically describes a vagal cardiac response to abdominal visceral stimulation. The ocular afferent pathway has a different name.
notes.B: A pressor reflex raises arterial pressure through cardiovascular effectors. It does not name the ocular trigeminovagal response.
notes.C: The Bezold–Jarisch reflex involves cardiac sensory afferents. The oculocardiac reflex begins with sensory input from ocular structures.
notes.E: The response can lower heart rate or pressure, but ‘depressor reflex’ is a general description rather than the specific eponym.

questions.stem: When the heart rate is 75 bt∙min-1, the duration of the cardiac cycle is:
questions.why: Cycle duration equals 60 seconds divided by beats per minute. At 75 beats per minute, the interval between corresponding points on successive beats is 0.8 seconds.

notes.A: A one-second cycle corresponds to 60 beats per minute, which is slower than the stated rate.
notes.B: A cycle duration of 0.6 seconds would give 100 beats per minute rather than 75.
notes.C: A 1.2-second cycle is equivalent to 50 beats per minute, which is slower than the rate given.
notes.E: One and a half seconds per cycle would produce 40 beats per minute, substantially below the stated rate.

questions.stem: Hyperaemia in skeletal muscle during exercise is normally associated with:

options.label: A
options.text: release of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone in the exercising muscles;

options.label: B
options.text: capillary dilation due to relaxation of capillary smooth muscle;

options.label: D
options.text: reflex vasoconstriction in other vascular beds;

questions.why: During exercise, sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood from splanchnic, renal and inactive tissues, which helps send cardiac output to the dilated active muscles.

notes.A: Sympathetic outflow to exercising muscle actually rises, but local metabolites override it (functional sympatholysis).
notes.B: Capillaries have no smooth muscle; arterioles and precapillary sphincters relax.
notes.C: Arterial pressure rises.
notes.E: The muscle pump and venous valves keep venous pressure in exercising limbs low.

questions.stem: Sinoatrial node cells are:

options.label: C
options.text: unable to generate impulses when completely denervated;

options.label: D
options.text: connected to the AV node by fine bundles of Purkinje tissue;

options.label: E
options.text: able to self generate impulses because their membrane potential is unstable.

questions.why: Sinoatrial nodal cells lack a stable resting membrane potential. Their diastolic depolarisation reaches threshold spontaneously, allowing them to generate impulses even without extrinsic autonomic input.

notes.A: The sinoatrial node is located in the right atrium near the superior vena cava. Its impulses spread to both atria.
notes.B: Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres modulate the node. Its extrinsic innervation is autonomic rather than somatic.
notes.C: Denervated nodal cells still depolarise spontaneously. Neural input changes the rate and does not provide the initiating impulse.
notes.D: Excitation passes to the atrioventricular node through atrial conduction pathways. The Purkinje network distributes excitation within the ventricles.

questions.stem: The first heart sound corresponds in time with:

options.label: A
options.text: closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves;

options.label: B
options.text: the P wave of the electrocardiogram;

options.label: E
options.text: the A wave in central venous pressure.

questions.why: The first heart sound occurs when rising ventricular pressure closes the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole. It accompanies early isovolumetric contraction.

notes.A: Aortic and pulmonary valve closure produces the second heart sound near the end of ventricular ejection.
notes.B: The P wave represents atrial electrical activation, which precedes the ventricular pressure rise and first sound.
notes.C: The immediate mechanical event is closure of the atrioventricular valves as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure.
notes.E: The central venous a wave is produced by atrial contraction before ventricular systole and the first heart sound.

questions.stem: The long absolute refractory period of cardiac muscle is important because it:

options.label: A
options.text: allows the atria and ventricles to contract at the same time;

options.label: B
options.text: shortens the time available for ventricular filling;

options.label: C
options.text: allows contractions to summate during heavy exercise;

options.label: D
options.text: prevents tetanic (sustained) contraction of the heart;

options.label: E
options.text: makes the ventricles more sensitive to premature stimuli.

questions.why: The long cardiac refractory period overlaps most of the contraction. This prevents repeated excitation from summating into tetany and preserves relaxation and filling between successive beats.

notes.A: Atrial and ventricular sequence depends on conduction timing, particularly the atrioventricular delay. Refractoriness prevents repeated excitation within a beat.
notes.B: Refractoriness limits re-excitation during systole. Filling depends on diastolic duration and opening of the inflow valves.
notes.C: Even during exercise, refractoriness limits temporal summation. The heart increases output by changing rate, filling and force.
notes.E: A refractory ventricle is temporarily less responsive to premature stimuli, and during absolute refractoriness it cannot be re-excited.

questions.stem: The strength of contraction of left ventricular muscle increases when:
questions.why: Greater left ventricular filling can increase end-diastolic fibre length. Within the physiological range, the Frank–Starling response increases active force at a given state of contractility.

notes.B: Higher extracellular potassium alters membrane potential and can impair excitation at marked elevations. It is not the normal preload stimulus.
notes.C: Lower extracellular calcium generally reduces calcium available for excitation–contraction coupling rather than increasing developed force.
notes.D: Magnesium changes can affect electrical stability and calcium handling. A fall is not the standard mechanism linking filling to force.
notes.E: Lower peripheral resistance can make ejection easier by reducing afterload. It does not increase initial stretch in the way greater filling does.

questions.stem: When parasympaticus is activated, there is:
questions.why: Cardiac parasympathetic activity slows the sinoatrial pacemaker through acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors. It can also increase the conduction delay through the atrioventricular node.

notes.A: Cardiac vagal activity primarily changes nodal behaviour. Hypertension is not the characteristic direct response.
notes.B: Tachycardia is a faster rate, whereas vagal input reduces the rate of spontaneous nodal firing.
notes.D: A longer filling interval can influence stroke volume indirectly. Bradycardia is the characteristic direct effect of cardiac vagal stimulation.
notes.E: Slowing of sinoatrial discharge is a recognised parasympathetic effect and has a corresponding choice.

questions.stem: Cardiac output:

options.label: A
options.text: is normally expressed as the output of each of the ventricles in litre/minute-1;

options.label: E
options.text: does not increase in exercise following denervation of the heart.

questions.why: Cardiac output is the volume pumped by either ventricle per minute. It equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate and is normally expressed in litres per minute.

notes.B: A resting adult typically has output nearer five litres per minute. Two litres per minute is low for many adults.
notes.C: Ten litres per minute can occur at higher demand. It is above the standard value used for resting adult physiology.
notes.D: Cold exposure can affect haemodynamics through several reflex and metabolic pathways. An increase is not the defining behaviour of cardiac output.
notes.E: A denervated heart can increase output through increased filling and circulating catecholamines. The response loses rapid direct neural adjustments.

questions.stem: In the brachial artery:

options.label: A
options.text: pulse waves travel at the same velocity as blood;

options.label: B
options.text: pulse pressure falls with decreasing elasticity of the wall;

options.label: C
options.text: pressure rises markedly when the artery is occluded distally;

options.label: D
options.text: pressure falls when the arm is raised above head level;

options.label: E
options.text: pulse pressures have a smaller amplitude than aortic pulse pressures.

questions.why: Raising the arm above heart level lowers local arterial pressure through the hydrostatic height difference. The brachial arterial pulse wave is a separate travelling pressure disturbance.

notes.A: The arterial pressure wave travels faster than the average movement of blood. Wave speed and flow velocity are distinct quantities.
notes.B: A stiffer arterial wall generally has lower compliance. For a given ejected volume, reduced compliance can increase pulse pressure.
notes.C: Distal occlusion stops downstream flow and alters reflections. It does not require a marked elevation of proximal mean pressure.
notes.E: Peripheral pulse pressure can exceed central aortic pulse pressure because of wave transmission and reflection along the arterial tree.

questions.stem: From functional point of view arterioles:

options.label: A
options.text: allow exchange of water, salts, electrolytes, hormones and other substances between plasma and tissues in both directions;

options.label: B
options.text: contain bigger part of the blood volume;

options.label: C
options.text: decrease the big fluctuations in blood plasma during the cardiac cycle;

options.label: D
options.text: form the resistance against the ventricular contractions;

options.label: E
options.text: play the role of reservoirs of blood from the capillaries.

questions.why: Arterioles are the main resistance vessels. Their smooth-muscle tone creates the largest pressure drop in the circulation, sets total peripheral resistance (the afterload against which the ventricles eject) and controls flow into capillary beds.

notes.A: Exchange is a capillary function.
notes.B: Veins hold most of the blood.
notes.C: Smoothing of pressure fluctuations is mainly done by the elastic arteries (Windkessel effect).
notes.E: Veins are the blood reservoirs.

questions.stem: In a denervated heart, the left ventricular stroke volume increases when the:

options.label: A
options.text: end-diastolic length of the ventricular fibres increases;

questions.why: Without nerves, the heart still adjusts stroke volume intrinsically. Greater end-diastolic fibre length gives a stronger contraction (Frank-Starling), so stroke volume rises.

notes.B: Lower resistance can raise stroke volume briefly, but stroke volume cannot stay above venous return; A is the main intrinsic mechanism.
notes.C: Falling blood volume reduces filling and stroke volume.
notes.D: Lower RV output reduces LV filling.
notes.E: Venodilation pools blood and reduces venous return.

questions.stem: As blood travels from the aorta towards the small peripheral arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: the arterial wall contains relatively more elastic tissue;

options.label: B
options.text: the flow becomes more likely to be turbulent;

options.label: C
options.text: the arterial pulse pressure tends to increase;

options.label: D
options.text: the mean arterial pressure rises slightly;

options.label: E
options.text: the arterial blood pO₂ falls appreciably.

questions.why: In healthy arteries pulse pressure often increases between the proximal aorta and peripheral muscular vessels. Changes in stiffness and wave reflections can amplify the systolic pressure excursion.

notes.A: The proximal aorta has abundant elastin. Farther away, distributing arteries are generally more muscular and less elastic.
notes.B: Smaller arterial size does not by itself establish more turbulence. Vessel diameter, flow velocity and viscosity all influence the tendency.
notes.D: Mean arterial pressure falls along the circuit as pressure energy is dissipated, even though the pulse amplitude can increase.
notes.E: Substantial oxygen exchange occurs mainly in the microcirculation. The pressure changes in distributing arteries do not imply major oxygen loss.

questions.stem: The heart rate is decreased when:
questions.why: Stimulating cardiac vagal fibres slows sinoatrial pacemaking through muscarinic receptors. If stimulation is strong, it can also slow transmission through the atrioventricular node.

notes.A: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and removes vagal slowing. It commonly increases the heart rate rather than reducing it.
notes.C: Glucocorticoids affect metabolism and vascular responsiveness. They are not the usual immediate physiological signal for slowing sinus rate.
notes.D: Calcium influences excitation–contraction coupling and can affect rhythm. It is not the standard direct intervention for physiological vagal slowing.
notes.E: Adrenaline stimulates cardiac beta receptors, usually accelerating sinoatrial discharge and increasing myocardial force.

questions.stem: Systemic hypertension may be caused by:

options.label: A
options.text: hypoxia due to chronic respiratory failure;

options.label: D
options.text: myocardial thickening (hypertrophy) of the left ventricle;

options.label: E
options.text: the rapid cardiac action of ventricular fibrillation.

questions.why: Excess aldosterone promotes renal sodium retention and can expand extracellular volume. These effects contribute to sustained systemic hypertension in conditions such as primary aldosteronism.

notes.A: Chronic alveolar hypoxia characteristically raises pulmonary vascular resistance. It more directly supports pulmonary rather than primary systemic hypertension in this comparison.
notes.C: Hyperinsulinaemia can accompany metabolic risk, but autonomous aldosterone excess is a direct established cause of secondary hypertension.
notes.D: Left ventricular hypertrophy is often a consequence of long-standing systemic pressure load. It is not itself the endocrine cause described here.
notes.E: Ventricular fibrillation prevents effective ventricular ejection. Arterial pressure collapses instead of rising from an effective rapid output.

questions.subtopic: Determinants and long-term control of pressure

questions.stem: The main factor, determining the diastolic blood pressure is:

options.label: E
options.text: the length of the blood vessel.

questions.why: During diastole arterial pressure falls as blood runs into peripheral vessels. Peripheral vascular resistance helps determine how rapidly that runoff occurs and how much pressure is maintained.

notes.A: Blood volume affects filling and pressure overall. It does not specifically describe resistance to diastolic runoff from the arterial compartment.
notes.B: Viscosity influences vascular resistance. The overall resistance of peripheral beds is the more direct determinant in this comparison.
notes.C: Ventricular ejection produces the arterial pressure rise and determines the amount ejected per beat. The rate of diastolic runoff depends mainly on vascular resistance and arterial compliance.
notes.E: Vessel length contributes to resistance but usually does not change quickly. Peripheral resistance integrates length, calibre and other factors.

questions.subtopic: Determinants and long-term control of pressure

questions.stem: In atrial fibrillation:

options.label: A
options.text: the electrocardiogram shows no evidence of atrial activity;

options.label: B
options.text: the ventricular rate is lower than atrial rate;

options.label: C
options.text: respiratory sinus arrhythmia can usually be registered;

options.label: D
options.text: the ventricular rate is higher than atrial rate;

options.label: E
options.text: the QRS complex has abnormal configuration.

questions.why: During atrial fibrillation, atrial activity is rapid and disorganised. The atrioventricular node conducts only some of those impulses, so ventricular activation is slower and usually irregular.

notes.A: Discrete P waves are absent, but fibrillatory activity can be visible in the baseline. The atria still generate electrical activity.
notes.C: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia depends on sinus-driven beats. Ventricular irregularity during atrial fibrillation instead reflects variable conduction.
notes.D: Atrial electrical activity can be several hundred impulses per minute. The atrioventricular node normally limits the number reaching the ventricles.
notes.E: QRS complexes can remain narrow when ventricular conduction is otherwise normal. A wide or abnormal complex is not required.

questions.stem: Fenestrated capillaries:

options.label: B
options.text: are located in most of the tissues;

options.label: C
options.text: permit only one-way exchange of materials;

options.label: D
options.text: have a layer of smooth muscle in their walls;

options.label: E
options.text: are found in the liver and kidneys.

questions.why: Fenestrated capillary endothelium contains pores that facilitate rapid exchange of water and small solutes. The capillary wall remains thin and lacks a continuous smooth muscle coat.

notes.B: Continuous capillaries are more widespread. Fenestrated capillaries specialise in exchange in tissues such as renal glomeruli and endocrine organs.
notes.C: Exchange follows pressure and concentration gradients and can occur in either direction. Fenestrations do not form one-way valves.
notes.D: Capillaries have an endothelial wall and basal lamina. They lack the smooth muscle coat characteristic of arterioles.
notes.E: Glomerular capillaries are classically fenestrated. Hepatic sinusoids also have pores but are conventionally classified as discontinuous capillaries.

questions.stem: The mean arterial blood pressure is about:

options.label: A
options.text: close in value to systolic, rather than the diastolic;

options.label: B
options.text: the average of systolic and diastolic blood pressure;

options.label: C
options.text: the diastolic plus one third of the pulse pressure

options.label: D
options.text: the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures;

options.label: E
options.text: the systolic plus one third of the diastolic pressure.

questions.why: At ordinary resting rates, mean arterial pressure can be estimated as diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure. The estimate reflects the relatively longer time spent in diastole.

notes.A: At ordinary resting rates, pressure spends more time lower in the cycle, so the mean is usually closer to diastolic pressure.
notes.B: The simple arithmetic average weights peak and trough equally. The actual mean is a time average over the pressure waveform.
notes.D: Subtracting diastolic pressure from systolic pressure gives pulse pressure, which measures the size of the pressure excursion.
notes.E: Adding a fraction of diastolic pressure to systolic pressure can exceed the peak. The mean lies between systolic and diastolic pressures.

questions.stem: The cardiac output (C.O.) is best defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: the volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle in each beat;

options.label: B
options.text: the volume of blood pumped by both ventricles together per minute;

options.label: C
options.text: the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute;

options.label: D
options.text: the volume of blood in each ventricle at the end of diastole;

options.label: E
options.text: the volume of blood left in each ventricle at the end of systole.

questions.why: Cardiac output is the volume ejected by one ventricle per unit time. It is obtained by multiplying the amount ejected per beat by beats per minute.

notes.A: Volume ejected in one beat is stroke volume. To obtain cardiac output it must be multiplied by heart rate.
notes.B: The ventricles pump in series, so adding their outputs would count flow through both sides of the same circulation twice.
notes.D: End-diastolic volume is the amount in the ventricle before contraction, not the volume delivered over a minute.
notes.E: End-systolic volume is what remains after ejection. Cardiac output measures the amount ejected per minute.

questions.stem: The velocity of arterial pulse conduction:

options.label: A
options.text: depends on the blood flow velocity;

options.label: B
options.text: is equal for the big and small arteries;

options.label: C
options.text: depends on the arterial wall peculiarities;

options.label: E
options.text: in lower in the smaller arteries.

questions.why: Pulse-wave velocity describes propagation of pressure along arterial walls. It depends strongly on wall stiffness and geometry, so it differs between vascular segments and changes with age.

notes.A: Blood flow velocity is the motion of fluid. The arterial pulse is a pressure disturbance that can travel much faster.
notes.B: Arterial segments differ in calibre and stiffness. Their pulse waves therefore do not all travel at the same speed.
notes.D: Arterial stiffness typically increases with age, which raises pulse-wave velocity even if mean blood flow is unchanged.
notes.E: Peripheral muscular arteries are often less distensible than the proximal aorta. Their pulse-wave speeds need not be lower.

questions.stem: Hardening of the arterial walls tends to raise:
questions.why: Stiffer arteries expand less for a given stroke volume. This tends to increase systolic pressure and widen pulse pressure, particularly as large elastic arteries stiffen with age.

notes.A: Hardening decreases arterial compliance. More pressure is required to produce the same change in arterial volume.
notes.C: Diastolic pressure does not necessarily rise with large-artery stiffness. Reduced elastic buffering commonly widens pulse pressure instead.
notes.D: Total peripheral resistance is governed mainly by resistance-vessel calibre. Large-artery stiffness acts strongly on pulsatile pressure and ventricular load.
notes.E: Breathing frequency is regulated by respiratory neural and chemical feedback. It is not the principal consequence of arterial stiffening.

questions.stem: Left ventricular failure tends to cause an increase in:

options.label: E
options.text: pulmonary oedema when the patient stands up.

questions.why: Left ventricular failure can raise left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure. The rise is transmitted to pulmonary capillaries, increasing the hydrostatic drive for pulmonary oedema.

notes.A: Right atrial pressure can rise if right-sided dysfunction develops later. The more direct effect of left ventricular failure is pulmonary congestion.
notes.B: Ejection fraction can be reduced or preserved in left-sided heart failure. It does not characteristically increase as the ventricle fails.
notes.D: Pulmonary congestion and interstitial oedema make lungs harder to inflate. Lung compliance generally falls rather than increases.
notes.E: Pulmonary oedema is driven by elevated capillary pressure. Standing is not the characteristic condition that causes it in left ventricular failure.

questions.stem: Which of following factors doesn't play role in the formation of the Effective Filtration Pressure in the capillaries:

options.label: B
options.text: the colloid osmotic pressure of plasma protein;

questions.why: Capillary fluid transfer depends on hydrostatic and oncotic forces across the microvascular barrier. Intrapleural pressure is not a separate direct force in the general transcapillary balance.

notes.A: Capillary blood pressure supplies an outward hydrostatic force that helps drive fluid into the interstitial compartment.
notes.B: Plasma proteins produce colloid osmotic pressure, which opposes outward fluid movement across the endothelial barrier.
notes.D: Hydrostatic pressure in surrounding tissue acts on the outside of the capillary and enters the pressure difference across its wall.
notes.E: The classical Starling model includes interstitial oncotic pressure. The revised model considers the protein concentration beneath the endothelial glycocalyx.

questions.stem: If the vagus nerve innervating the heart is blocked, than:

options.label: E
options.text: the heart activity would remain unchanged.

questions.why: The vagus normally restrains sinoatrial pacemaker rate at rest. Blocking vagal input removes that muscarinic inhibition, allowing the heart rate to rise toward its intrinsic value.

notes.A: A slower rate would follow increased vagal stimulation. Removing that influence produces the opposite pacemaker response.
notes.B: Stroke volume may change with filling time, but it is not the direct predictable result of loss of vagal input.
notes.C: Cardiac output depends on both rate and stroke volume. A fall is not the inevitable response to vagal blockade.
notes.E: Even though the heart has intrinsic automaticity, removing a tonic inhibitory input changes how rapidly it discharges.

questions.stem: The plateau phase of the action potential of the contractile myocardiocytes is due to:

options.label: A
options.text: the slow movement of Na+ across the cell membrane;

options.label: C
options.text: the increased membrane permeability to K+;

options.label: D
options.text: the increased membrane permeability to Na+;

options.label: E
options.text: a decrease in Ca2+ diffusing across membrane.

questions.why: Slow inward calcium current through L-type channels helps sustain the plateau in a contractile myocyte. It counterbalances outward potassium current and contributes to excitation–contraction coupling.

notes.A: Sodium influx produces the rapid upstroke in working ventricular cells. It is not the principal inward current sustaining the plateau.
notes.C: Outward potassium currents help repolarise the membrane. During the plateau they are balanced in part by inward calcium current.
notes.D: Fast sodium channels increase sodium permeability during phase zero and then inactivate. The plateau follows that brief event.
notes.E: The plateau depends on continued calcium entry. Declining inward current helps allow outward potassium current to repolarise the cell.
